DHAMMAPADA.

FROM THREE MANUSCRIPTS IN COPENHAGEN

EDITED IN PALI,

TRANSLATED INTO LATIN, WITH EXCERPTS FROM THE PALI COMMENTARY

AND ILLUSTRATED WITH NOTES

BY V. FAUSBÖLL.

COPENHAGEN
PUBLISHED BY THE HEIRS OF REITZEL.

LEIPZIG
PUBLISHED BY LORCK.

LONDON
PUBLISHED BY WILLIAMS & NORGATE.

1855.

To the most kind and most distinguished gentlemen,

M. Hammerich,
Professor, Rector of the School,

and

N. L. Westergaard,
Professor of Laws, Knight of the Order of Dannebrog,

the best teachers, to be revered with devotion,

each of whom, with the greatest benevolence, came to the aid of my own very slight powers,

this book

the most devoted author

wished to be dedicated.

IV.

...poured forth, and brought the first beginnings of the arts to the Tibetans and Mongols, to India beyond the Ganges, and to the island of Taprobane, so that today it has as followers almost a third part of the human race, and the institutions, languages, and other features of those lands can scarcely be understood unless the language held sacred to that religion is first known.d

Since these things were so, I resolved that I would, to the best of my ability, work at communicating with learned men through these letters. And to make a beginning, I chose, on the advice of the distinguished Westergaard, the book called the Dhammapada,e because among the manuscripts brought by Rask three copies of it existed, one of which was furnished with a commentary.

These three manuscripts, in the first part of the catalogue of Oriental manuscripts...

[footnote continuation, in English in the original:]
...hending under this appellation, 1st, the Dulvá (Vinaya); 2ndly, the Do (Sútra); 3rdly, the Sher-ch'hin (Abhidharmah).'

d Compare La Loubère: Description of the Kingdom of Siam. Amsterdam, 1700, vol. I p. 26:

'The terms of Religion and of Justice, the names of Offices, and all the ornaments of the vernacular language are borrowed from Bali [Pali]. They even compose their finest songs in Bali, etc.'

Taylor Jones, quoted in Weber: Indische Studien, vol. II, p. 320:

'Nearly half the words of the (Siamese) language borrow a tinge or shade of meaning from their connection with Buddhism. A general and somewhat accurate view of this system is therefore essential to a good knowledge of the language. Without it a student gains only an approximation, often quite remote, to the true import of terms.'

e Compare Knighton: The History of Ceylon, p. 77:

'In the "Damma Padan," or the "Footsteps of Religion," we have exemplified a code of morality, and a list of precepts which, for pureness, excellence and wisdom, is only second to that of the Divine Lawgiver himself.'

Spence Hardy: Eastern Monachism, p. 169:

'A collection might be made from the precepts of this work, that in the purity of its ethics could scarcely be equalled from any other heathen author.'

VI

I have therefore published this text just as it is transmitted among the Sinhalese, because I judge that in a first edition the traces of the tradition ought to be followed. In the Notes and Appendix, however, I have tried as far as I could to point out the errors, and in a second edition this will have to be attended to, so that the text may be restored to its integrity as far as possible.

Among the sacred Buddhist writings this book seems to be counted among the older ones, as appears from the language it uses, which in many respects is far removed from the Sanskritic—and indeed from the most ancient form of it—and differs greatly in style from that used by the prose Suttas and the commentaries of Buddhaghosa. Here belong: the present active participle nominative in -am, as ganayam, rodam; the 3rd person plural present middle in -are, as socare, upapajjare; the dative gerund, as netave, pahátave; and besides these, forms such as: karoto and kubbato (karontassa), káhiti (karissati) and others, arahatam (arahantánam), sabbhi (santehi), vaddha (vuddha), klesa (kilesa), cetya (cetiya), etc. It is also worth noting that the sentences deal solely with ethical matter and concern individual persons, not human society as a whole. Nor does it seem out of place, when inquiring into the period at which this book appeared, to note the use of the word "nirutti" in verse 352, and that only the following divine names occur: Deva (vv. 30, 56, 94, 105, 181, 200, 224, 230, 366, 420, 177), Gandhabba (vv. 105, 420), Ábhassara (v. 200), Mára (vv. 7, 8, 34, 37, 40, 46, 57, 105, 175, 274, 337, 350), Yama (vv. 235, 237, 44), Brahman (vv. 105, 230), Maghavan (v. 30).

The Dhammapada appears to be older than the Suttanipáta, which not only frequently repeats phrases found in the Dhammapada, but has also borrowed whole verses from it (125, 205, 326, 353, 396–423), as well as half-verses (pádas) of many lines (5, 20, 129, 141, 142, 170, 185, 239, 289, 315, 340, 345, 364, 367, 375). Indeed—unless I am mistaken—the Dhammapada quotes this very verse:

VII

He who, well-taught in the Dhammapada,
lives on the path, restrained and mindful,
following blameless ways,
of him they say he is truly a liver of the path.

Moreover, I found in the Játaka likewise a number of verses of the Dhammapada (as at 4, 5, 21, 328–330, 845, attached now to the same, now to different stories), which it seems probable to me were transferred from the Játaka into the Dhammapada; unless perhaps it must be supposed that both books flowed from a common source, for the verses of both the Dhammapada and the Játaka are in truth fragments of older writings, which Gotama the Samana excerpted with an ethical purpose in view. Whether the word Pátimokkha in verses 185 and 375 denotes the book of that name or not is not sufficiently clear.

As for the title of the book, Dhammapadam, having regard to verses 44 and 101, I interpret it thus, that it signifies "A Collection of Verses on Religion"; for the word pada, because of the verb pacessati in verse 44, must be understood collectively, and gáthápadam in verse 101 seems to show that the word pada carries the notion of "verse." It is possible, however, that the word pada should be assigned the meaning of "word" or "sentence." Gogerly translates it: The Footsteps of Religion; compare verse 91.

As for what I have excerpted from the commentary of Buddhaghosa, since reliance must be placed on only one manuscript, it cannot but fall far short of completeness. For the manuscript, though not a bad one, is nevertheless, not to mention the many individual errors, inconsistent, first of all, as most Sinhalese manuscripts are, in determining the quantity of the vowels i and u, especially in terminations; in this matter indeed, having noted the manuscript's spelling, I had resolved always to follow the rules of the Pali grammarians, but since some of these rules are contradicted by the consistent testimony of this manuscript and of the greater part of other manuscripts, owing to the doubt which has always beset me on this point, setting aside my own judgment, I have sometimes left the manuscript's spelling untouched. Furthermore

VIII

There is likewise uncertainty in distinguishing the nasals ṇ and ṅ; since the Pali grammarians prescribe nothing on this matter, and the Pali dialect surely follows different rules than Sanskrit (thus it easily appears that the sound r in a word, when it precedes, does not always require transmutation of n into ṇ in the terminations of inflection, e.g. assúni or açrúni, except in tíṇi, and in the derivative syllable -in, e.g. averino or avairinas); it would have been proper for me to investigate in each individual word what the common spelling was, and thus I wrote, with n, e.g. savana, nikkhamana, nibbána, pahína, etc., and with ṇ, e.g. pamáṇa, khíṇa, pahiṇi, pápuṇati, sakkuṇáti, áṇápesi (one would expect aññápesi, cf. Anecdota Pali, ed. Spiegel p. 72), etc.; I hesitated, however, between the forms ñáṇa and ñáṇa, of which, although the former is by far the more frequent, I did not dare to reject the latter on account of Sanskrit usage. To reduce to a rule the entire use of the sound ṇ and of the vowels í and ú cannot be done until more books have been published, since the manuscripts are very poor in these matters. The codex is also inconsistent as regards the doubling of a consonant in a compound word, when two consonants lie hidden at the beginning of the second word; it seems to me that the doubling should generally be kept, and so one should write, e.g., Ánandatthera, viṁññáṇa, parikkhitta, not Ánandathera, viñáṇa, parikhitta. Nor does the manuscript always distinguish accurately enough between ḷ and l; but I think, in my judgment, that ḷ should consistently be written whenever a ḍ or ḍh corresponds to it in the Sanskrit word corresponding to the Pali one — though not always, for which reason I wrote: kíḷati, ḍalha, guḷa, but gilati, ulára, antalikkha, etc. There are, besides, as will easily appear, other minor points equally doubtful, about which, however, lest I seem too verbose, I forbear to speak further.

As for my having published this book in Latin script, it scarcely needs a lengthy defense. For since the Pali letters now have no script of their own (though it is attested that they once had one, the Kammavácá), but instead use Burmese, Siamese, or Sinhalese script, it seems to me that nothing prevents us from using the Latin one; the Europeans...

X

...the liberality of the Danish [kingdom/realm] in promoting Oriental studies, which is celebrated even among foreigners, was also of great assistance to me, since my affairs were watched over by the distinguished gentlemen presiding over the Ministry of Public Worship and Education, Madvig, Simony, and Bang. Thanks are also due to the most learned sub-rector of classical literature at Frederiksborg, Ostermann, who, not unskilled in the Sanskrit language, helped me greatly in rendering the text into Latin; moreover to the most kind and dear-to-me gentlemen Fabricius-Möller and A. K. Greib, who assisted me in various ways, but especially to the most learned linguist Trecknero, with whose help I was able to correct and emend a great many things while the book was being printed and proofed. Finally, I ought to make mention of the remarkable goodwill with which the men attached to the libraries of this city aided my work, and especially worthy of praise is the generosity by which the prefects of these libraries, the distinguished gentlemen Werlauff, Privy Councillor of Conferences, and Thorsen, Professor, granted me the use of manuscripts and books.

If it should appear that I have not spent vain effort in working on this book, then besides some lesser works, a greater work, the Jātaka, will follow. So farewell, kind reader, and look favorably upon me!

Written at Copenhagen on the Ides of March, 1855.

HOMAGE

TO THAT BLESSED ONE, THE WORTHY ONE, THE FULLY ENLIGHTENED ONE.

1. The Chapter of Pairs.

1. All phenomena are preceded by mind, mind is their chief, they are made by mind;
if one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind,
suffering follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws (the cart).

2. All phenomena are preceded by mind, mind is their chief, they are made by mind;
if one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows him, like a shadow that never departs.

3. "He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me" —
in those who harbor such thoughts, hatred is never appeased.

4. "He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me" —
in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred is appeased.

Chapter 1.

1. Natures take their origin from the mind; the mind is the more important part
of them, they consist of mind; if (one) speaks or acts with a defiled mind,
then pain follows him, as the track (of the wheel follows) the foot of the ox
2. drawing (the cart). Natures from the mind etc.; if (one) with a serene mind
speaks or acts, then joy follows him,
3. like a shadow that never departs. "He has overwhelmed me with abuse, he has done violence to me,
he has conquered me, he has despoiled me" — those who clothe themselves with that disposition,
4. their anger is not calmed. Abuse etc.; those
who do not clothe themselves with that disposition, their anger is calmed among them.

1

3

12. Having known the essential as essential and the non-essential as non-essential,
they reach the essential, moving in the sphere of right thought.

13. As rain breaks through a badly thatched house,
so passion breaks through an uncultivated mind.

14. As rain does not break through a well-thatched house,
so passion does not break through a well-cultivated mind.

15. Here he grieves, after death he grieves,
the evildoer grieves in both places;
he grieves, he is afflicted,
seeing the impurity of his own deeds.

16. Here he rejoices, after death he rejoices,
the doer of good rejoices in both places;
he rejoices, he exceedingly rejoices,
seeing the purity of his own deeds.

17. Here he suffers torment, after death he suffers torment,
the evildoer suffers torment in both places;
"Evil has been done by me," thus he suffers torment,
he suffers torment even more, having gone to a bad state.

11. ...deserves the yellow robe. In this, that, considering the non-essential
as essential, and seeing the essential as non-essential,
these do not attain to the essential, being companions of false pursuit.

12. But those who hold the essential as essential, and the non-essential
as non-essential, these attain to the essential, being companions of true pursuit.

13. As rain breaks through a badly roofed house, so desire breaks through
a mind destitute of meditation.

14. As rain does not break through a well-roofed house, so desire
does not break through

15. a meditative mind. In this life he who does evil grieves; having died, he grieves;
he grieves in both places; he grieves, he is saddened, seeing the misery of

16. his own wrongdoing. In this life he who does good rejoices; having died, he rejoices...

4

18. Here he rejoices, and after death he rejoices,
the doer of merit rejoices in both places;
"Merit has been made by me," thus he rejoices;
he rejoices all the more when gone to a happy state.

19. Even if reciting much sacred text,
the heedless man who is not a doer [of what he recites]
is like a cowherd counting the cattle of others —
he has no share in the fruit of the holy life.

20. Even if reciting little of the sacred text,
one who lives in accordance with the Dhamma,
having abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion,
possessed of right knowledge, with mind well freed,
clinging to nothing here or beyond —
he has a share in the fruit of the holy life.

End of the First Chapter, the Chapter of Pairs.

[Latin commentary portion:]

...he who has done good rejoices in both places; he rejoices, he rejoices greatly,
17. rejoicing as he sees the purity of his own deed. In this life the doer of evil is tormented; having died, he is tormented; he is tormented in both places. Thinking, "Evil has been done by me," thus he is tormented;
18. he is tormented all the more once he has entered hell. In this life he rejoices; having died, he who has done good rejoices; he rejoices in both places. Thinking, "Good has been done by me," thus he rejoices, and he rejoices all the more
19. once he has entered heaven. Likewise, even if a careless man speaks many wholesome words, he does not act accordingly — like a herdsman who counts the cattle of others,
20. he does not become a sharer in the community. Likewise, even if someone speaks only a few wholesome words, if he lives his life according to the law, and having abandoned desire and hatred and mental disturbance, is truly wise, endowed with a mind well freed through right reflection, desiring nothing either here or there — he becomes a sharer in the community.

5

2. The Chapter on Heedfulness.

21. Heedfulness is the path to the deathless, heedlessness is the path to death; the heedful do not die, but the heedless are as if dead already.

22. Having clearly understood this distinction, the wise who are heedful rejoice in heedfulness, delighting in the sphere of the noble ones.

23. They, meditative, steadfast, ever firm in their effort, the wise touch Nibbana, the unsurpassed freedom from bondage.

24. For one who is energetic, mindful, pure in action, careful and deliberate in deeds, self-restrained, living righteously, and heedful — his glory increases.

25. By effort, heedfulness, self-restraint, and self-control, let the wise one build for himself an island that no flood can overwhelm.

26. Fools, unwise people, give themselves over to heedlessness; but the wise one guards heedfulness as his greatest treasure.


Chapter 2.

21. Vigilance is the road to immortality, sloth is the road to death; those who are vigilant do not die, while the slothful are as if already dead.
22. (They are dead.) Understanding this distinction clearly, those skilled in vigilance
23. rejoice in vigilance, delighting in the lot of the noble. These, meditative, persevering, ever endowed with strong powers, the wise attain Nibbana, the highest happiness. Through striving, remembering, laboring honestly, acting thoughtfully, restraining and composing themselves, and living piously, the glory of the vigilant increases.
24. By the exertion of their powers, through vigilance, self-restraint, and temperance, let the wise man make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
25. Fools, unwise men, pursue sloth; but the wise man guards vigilance as the best of treasures. Let no one...

7

3. The Chapter on the Mind.

33. The mind, flickering and fickle, hard to guard, hard to restrain — the wise man makes it straight, as a fletcher straightens an arrow shaft.

34. Like a fish thrown onto dry land, drawn out of its watery home, this mind thrashes about, struggling to escape the dominion of Mára.

35. The restraint of a mind that is hard to hold, light, and prone to dart wherever it pleases is wholesome; a tamed mind brings happiness.

36. Let the wise man guard a mind that is hard to perceive and very subtle, one that glides wherever it wishes; a guarded mind brings happiness.

37. Those who will restrain the mind — which travels far, wanders alone, is bodiless, and lies hidden in the cave (of the heart) — will be freed from the bonds of Mára.

38. The wisdom of one whose mind is unsteady, who does not know the true Law, and whose faith is wavering, never reaches fullness.

———————————

Chapter 3.

33. The mind, luxuriant and fluctuating, hard to guard, hard to restrain — the wise man makes it straight, like a fletcher straightening an arrow.

34. Like a fish cast onto land, torn from its watery home, this mind flutters about, trying to escape the kingdom of Mára.

35. The restraint of a mind that is difficult to control, light, and apt to cast itself headlong wherever it likes is beneficial; a mind that is tamed brings joy.

36. Let the wise man watch over a mind that is hard to observe, very subtle, and prone to slip away wherever it pleases; a mind that is guarded brings joy.

37. Those who restrain the mind — which roams far, wanders alone, is without body, and dwells hidden (in the heart) — will be set free from the bonds of Mára.

38. The understanding of one whose mind is inconstant, who does not recognize the true Law, and whose confidence is unsteady, does not attain its full measure.

39. For those not endowed with a steady mind...

8

39. For one whose mind is not soaked (by passion), whose thoughts are not afflicted,
who has abandoned both merit and demerit — for such a one, being watchful, there is no fear.

40. Having known this body to be like a water-jar,
having established this mind like a fortified city,
one should attack Mára with the weapon of wisdom,
and should guard what has been conquered, and remain without attachment.

41. Before long, alas, this body
will lie upon the earth, cast away, devoid of consciousness,
like a useless log.

42. Whatever an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater,
a wrongly directed mind can do to oneself something even worse than that.

43. What neither mother nor father could do,
nor any other relatives,
a well-directed mind can do for oneself something better than that.

The Third Chapter: The Chapter on the Mind.


[Latin commentary, translated:]
Of one who has an unimpaired mind, free from both good and evil, who is watchful,
40. there is no fear. Recognizing this body as being like a jar, and establishing a thought like a fortress,
one (the wise person) should subdue
Mára with the weapons of understanding, and should guard what has been won, and be free of attachment (dwelling).
41. In a short time, alas, this body will lie
42. worthless on the ground, devoid of judgment, useless like a stick. Whatever an enemy
does to an enemy, or one full of hatred again to one full of hatred, —
43. a wrongly applied thought brings him still more harm than that. Not
what a mother or father would do, nor other relatives as well, —
— a rightly applied thought brings him still more good than that.

9

4. The Chapter on Flowers.

44. Who shall conquer this earth,
    and this world of Yama together with its gods?
    Who shall discern the well-taught verses of the Law,
    as a skilled person gathers flowers?
45. The disciple (Sekha) shall conquer this earth,
    and this world of Yama together with its gods;
    the disciple shall discern the well-taught verses of the Law,
    as a skilled person gathers flowers.
46. Knowing this body to be like froth,
    awakening to its mirage-like nature,
    having cut off the flower-shoots of Mára,
    one should go where the King of Death cannot see.
47. Death carries away, like a great flood sweeping off a sleeping village,
    the man whose mind clings to gathering flowers.
48. The Ender makes subject to his power
    the man whose mind clings to gathering flowers,
    who is never satisfied with sensual pleasures.

_______________________________________

Chapter 4.

44. Who shall conquer this earth and this world together with that of Yama and the gods? Who shall gather well-explained verses of the Law
45. as a skilled flower-gatherer gathers flowers? The disciple (Sekha) shall conquer this earth and this world together with that of Yama and the gods; the disciple shall gather the well-explained verses of the Law,
46. as a skilled flower-gatherer gathers flowers. Considering this body to be like foam, recognizing its nature to be like a mirage of sunbeams, and breaking off Mára's flower-tipped arrows,
47. the beggar (monk) shall not be seen by the king of death. Death carries off, as a flood carries off a sleeping village,
48. the man who gathers flowers, whose mind is attached (to sensual pleasures), never satisfied. Of the one who gathers flowers—

11

56. This fragrance is but slight, that of tagara and sandalwood;
but the fragrance of the virtuous wafts upward, supreme among the gods.

57. The path of those endowed with virtue, living heedfully,
freed through perfect knowledge — Mára cannot find it.

58. Just as upon a heap of rubbish thrown on the highway
a lotus might spring up there, sweetly fragrant and delightful;

59. so, among beings who are like rubbish, blind common folk,
the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One shines forth surpassingly through wisdom.

The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Flowers.

5. The Chapter on Fools.

60. Long is the night for one who is awake, long is a league for one who is weary,
long is the round of rebirth (saṁsára) for fools who do not know the true Law.

_______________________________________________

or even of tagara, of the blue lotus, and of jasmine — among these fragrant things, there is a finest fragrance, than which none is more excellent.

56. (Yet) slight indeed is this scent, which itself belongs to tagara and sandalwood; but the scent of the virtuous, that truly breathes among the gods,

57. is the most excellent. By the power of those adorned with these virtues, living vigilantly, because of their perfect knowledge, the freed ones — Mára

58. does not find their path. Just as in a dung-heap thrown by the great road a flower is born there, possessed of a pure fragrance,

59. gladdening the mind, so among the multitude that resembles filth, amid the blinded crowd, there shines forth, by intelligence, clearly, the disciple (listener) of the wise Buddha.

_______________

Chapter 5.

60. Long is the night for one who keeps watch, long is the road for one who is weary, long is the wandering (round of rebirth, saṁsára) of fools who do not understand the true Law.

12

61. If a traveler cannot find a companion better than or equal to himself, let him walk firmly alone, for there is no companionship with a fool.

62. "I have sons, I have wealth," thus thinking, the fool is troubled; indeed he himself does not belong to himself — how then sons, how then wealth?

63. The fool who knows his own folly is, by that very fact, wise to that extent; but the fool who thinks himself wise is the one truly called a "fool."

64. Even if a fool associates with a wise man all his life, he does not come to know the Dhamma, just as a spoon does not perceive the taste of soup.

65. But if a discerning person associates with a wise man even for a moment, he quickly comes to know the Dhamma, just as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.

66. Fools of little understanding go about as their own enemies, doing evil deeds, which bear bitter fruit.

67. That deed is not well done which, having been done, causes remorse, and whose result one experiences with a tearful face, weeping.

14

75. "One is the path that leads to gain, another is the path that leads to Nibbana" — having understood this, the monk, a disciple of the Buddha, should not delight in honors, but should cultivate solitude.

End of the Fifth Chapter, on the Fool.


6. The Chapter on the Wise.

76. One should associate with such a wise man as reveals hidden faults like a finder of treasure, who speaks words of reproof, who is wise and discerning; for one who associates with such a person, things turn out better, not worse.

77. Let him admonish, let him instruct, and let him restrain one from what is improper; for he who does so is dear to the good and displeasing to the wicked.

78. Let him not associate with evil friends, let him not associate with base men; let him associate with good friends, let him associate with the best of men.


...to be set aside, in whatever matter — such is how the fool's mind turns; his desire and arrogance increase. "One thing indeed is the pursuit of worldly gain, another is what looks toward Nibbana" — understanding this, the mendicant, a listener of the Buddha, does not desire honor, but cultivates solitude all the more.


Chapter 6.

76. Let him cultivate the kind of person who, like one who points out buried treasures, reveals faults, rebukes, and is wise and understanding; for one who cultivates such a person, it turns out better, not worse. Let such a one admonish, instruct, and restrain from what is unfitting; he indeed becomes a friend to the good and an enemy to the wicked.

78. Let him not cultivate wicked friends, let him not cultivate the basest of men; let him cultivate good friends, let him cultivate the best of men. One who absorbs the Law lives happily and serenely...

15

79. One who delights in the Dhamma sleeps happily with a serene mind; the wise person always rejoices in the Dhamma taught by the Noble Ones.

80. Irrigators lead water (where they wish); fletchers shape arrows; carpenters shape wood; the wise tame themselves.

81. As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by blame or praise.

82. Just as a deep lake is clear and undisturbed, so the wise become serene upon hearing the teachings.

83. Good people walk (their path) everywhere; the virtuous do not chatter out of desire for pleasures; touched by happiness or by pain, the wise show no difference (in their composure).

84. Not for one's own sake, nor for another's sake, should one desire a son, wealth, or a kingdom; one should not desire one's own prosperity by unrighteous means. Such a one is virtuous, wise, and righteous.

[Latin commentary, translated:]
By this contemplation, the wise person, always delighted by the law expounded by the venerable ones. (80) Water indeed is led by irrigators; archers' craftsmen fashion the arrow; carpenters shape wood; the wise tame themselves. (81) As a solid rock is not moved by the wind, so the wise do not waver amid blame and praise. (82) As a deep lake is serene and untroubled, so the wise are settled by hearing the laws. (83) Everywhere indeed good men move about; the virtuous, devoted to love, do not complain; touched by joy or likewise by sorrow, the wise show no varying disposition. (84) Not for his own sake, nor for another's sake does the wise man desire a son, nor wealth, nor a kingdom; he does not wish to increase his own (fortune) by wrongdoing; he is endowed with virtue, with wisdom,

16

85. Few among men are those people who reach the farther shore;
but the rest of this multitude only runs along the (near) bank.

86. But those who, acting in accordance with the Doctrine when it has been well taught,
those people will go to the farther shore, (crossing) the very hard-to-cross realm of death.

87. Having abandoned the dark doctrine, let the wise man cultivate the bright one;
having gone from home into homelessness, into solitude, where it is hard to find delight,

88. let him, having abandoned sensual pleasures, owning nothing, wish for delight there;
let the wise man purify himself from the defilements of the mind.

89. Those whose minds are well developed in the factors of enlightenment,
who, without clinging, delight in the relinquishing of attachment,
who have destroyed the corruptions and are full of light — they are, in this world, fully quenched.

The Sixth Chapter: the Chapter on the Wise.

———————————————————————

85. justice [continuing from previous page]. Few indeed are those among men who reach the farther shore; the rest, that great multitude, only run about on this (nearer) shore.

86. But those who live in conformity with the Doctrine when it has been well proclaimed, those people will reach the farther shore, crossing the realm of death, which is extremely hard to cross.

The commentary contained in codex B is so arranged that each verse (or sometimes several verses joined together) is preceded by a story, sometimes longer, sometimes shorter, which shows in what place, dwelling, and with regard to whom the Buddha delivered this teaching; the story ends with the verse, which is then followed by an interpretation of the words. So that you may clearly understand the method of the whole commentary, I shall now bring to light the complete commentary on the first verse. Afterwards, from the interpretation of the words, I shall extract the more important matters for each verse individually; the stories, however, are more numerous and often of greater extent than I could describe in full, nor do I think it necessary, since they are neither closely nor intimately connected with the verses, nor do they bear upon the doctrine delivered in the verses except in a general way, so that almost nothing of value for interpreting the verses results from them. I shall therefore make a selection of those especially which seem to contribute something toward illustrating the history. I have tried, as far as I could, to emend the text.

The people, not seeing the elder, asked, "Where has our chief gone?" and having heard what had happened, they sent rice-gruel, and themselves taking almsfood, went and worshipped the elder; falling at his feet, weeping, they said, "Venerable sir, we will look after you; do not grieve," and having comforted him thus, they departed.

From then on they continually sent rice-gruel and food to the monastery. The elder also constantly instructed the other sixty monks. Standing firm in his instruction, by the time of the near-Pavāraṇā ceremony, all of them together attained arahantship along with the analytical knowledges. Having completed the rains-residence, wishing to see the Teacher, they said to the elder, "Venerable sir, we wish to see the Teacher." Having heard their words, the elder thought: "I am weak, and on the road ahead there is a forest infested by non-human beings; if these monks travel with me, they will all become exhausted, and will not even be able to obtain alms. I shall send them on ahead." Then he said to them, "Friends, go on ahead." They said, "But what of you, venerable sir?" [He replied], "I am weak, and on the road ahead there is a forest infested by non-human beings; if you travel with me, you will all become exhausted. Go on ahead." [They said], "Venerable sir, do not say such a thing; we will never go without you." [He said], "Do not wish it so, friends; if that is how it is, it will be troublesome for me. My younger brother, upon seeing you, will ask after me; then you should tell him of the loss of my eyesight. He will send someone to fetch me, and I shall come together with him. In my name, pay homage to the Ten-Powered One and to the eighty great elders." Thus he sent them off. Having asked the elder's forgiveness, they entered the village. The people, having seated them and given them alms, asked, "Venerable sirs, is there some reason known for your going?" "Yes, lay devotees, we wish to see the Teacher." The people, having begged them again and again, and having realized their firm intention to go, followed after them lamenting, then turned back. The monks, in due course, went on to Jetavana, and having paid homage to the Teacher and the great elders (c. and the venerable ones) by the elder's instruction, [they] again...

On the day when they went into the street for alms where the elder's younger brother lived, the householder, recognizing them, had them sit down and, having made due hospitality, asked: "Where is my brother, the elder, now?" Then they told him the news, whereupon he, falling at their feet, wept and asked: "Venerable sirs, what should now be done?" The elder replied: "From here he is sending word to a certain village (so that when the time comes he will come together with him)." [The brother said:] "Venerable sir, this is my nephew named Pālita; please send him [to the elder]." [The elder said:] "It is not possible to send him in this way, for there is danger on the road; it would be better to have him ordained and then send him." [The brother said:] "Then do so and send him, venerable sir." So they had him ordained, and after training him for half a month in the handling of robes and other duties, they pointed out the road to him and sent him off.

Journeying on by stages, he reached that village, and at the village gate, seeing an old man, he asked him: "Is there any forest monastery depending on this village?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Who lives there?" "The elder Pālita, venerable sir." "Please show me the way." "Who are you?" "I am the nephew of the venerable elder." Then the old man took him and led him to the monastery. He paid homage to the elder, and after performing all his duties properly for half a month and attending on the elder well, he said: "Venerable sir, my uncle's household is longing for your coming; let us go." [The elder] said: "Well then, take hold of my staff." So, taking hold of the end of the staff, he entered the village together with the elder. The people, having seated them, asked: "Venerable sir, what is the reason for your coming known to you?" [He replied:] "Yes, lay devotees, we have come to pay homage to the Teacher."

Though the people begged him in many ways, they could not keep him; and as they saw the elder off, they went partway, then wept and turned back. The novice, carrying the end of the elder's staff (or: taking it), went on; and on the way, in the forest, the elder reached Katthanañgara, a village which he had previously frequented as his resting place. Going out from there into the forest, while cutting wood and singing, the novice heard the song of a certain woman who was gathering firewood, and took the sound as an object of fascination. There is said to be no other sound among men capable of so pervading and seizing hold of a man's whole body as the sound of a woman's voice. Hence the Blessed One said: "Monks, I know of no other single sound that so seizes and holds a man's mind captive as this, monks -- the sound of a woman."

The novice, having taken up the pretext there and thrown down his bundle of sticks, said, "Wait here a while, sir, I have something to attend to," and went to her side.

She, seeing him, fell silent, and he with her fell into a breach of moral conduct.

The elder thought: "Just now there was the sound of singing — where was it heard? It was from a woman. Could it be that the novice too has fallen into a breach of morality?"

He, having finished his business, came back and said, "Let us go now, sir."

Then the elder asked him, "Novice, have you become corrupt?" He, falling silent, said nothing even when asked again and again.

Then the elder said, "With one so corrupt as you, I have no further business of traveling together."

He, struck with remorse, removed his ochre robes and dressed himself as a layman would, saying: "Sir, I was formerly a novice, but now I have become a layman. Even when I went forth, I did not do so out of faith, but out of fear of the dangers of the road. Come, let us go" — so he said.

[The elder replied:] "Friend, a wicked layman is wicked, and a wicked monk is likewise wicked. Having stood even in the state of a monk, you were unable to fulfill mere morality — having become a layman, what good, indeed, will you do? With one so corrupt as you, I have no business of traveling together."

"But sir, the road is beset by non-human dangers, and you are blind besides — how will you manage here?"

Then the elder said: "Friend, do not think in this way. Even if I should lie down right here and die, or even if I go on and on, there is no going together with you" — and having said this, he spoke these verses:

"Here am I, with my eyes destroyed, come into the midst of the wilderness road; I will not go on like this(?) — there is no companionship with a fool."

"Here am I, with my eyes destroyed, come into the midst of the wilderness road; I shall die, I shall not go on — there is no companionship with a fool."

Hearing this, the other was struck with remorse, thinking, "Indeed, a grave and improper deed has been done by me" — and raising his arms, weeping, he plunged into the forest thicket and went off just so.

Then, by the power of the elder's virtue, there arose [a wondrous seat] sixty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in breadth, and fifteen yojanas thick, the color of jayasumana flowers, pleasant and agreeable to sit upon and rise from...

Having had a leaf-hut built and having had him (the Thera) seated on a couch, [she sent word] through her dear companion to his presence; having gone and called out, "Sammā Pālā!" (or "Sammā!") — "What is it, Sammā?" Knowing that the Thera had arrived, [but pretending not to], [he said] "I do not know; but has the Thera really come?" "Yes, Sammā; just now, having gone to the monastery, I saw the Thera sitting in the leaf-hut you had built, and I came back saying, 'He is here.'" So saying, he went off. The householder too, having gone to the monastery and seen the Thera, bowed at his feet and said, "Seeing this, Lord, I wish you to ordain me" — and having spoken such words, he set free two slaves as freedmen, and had him ordained in the Thera's presence. He had rice-gruel, food, and so on brought from within the village, and arranged for someone to wait upon the Thera; the novices performed their duties and attended upon the Thera.

Then one day, monks from various districts, thinking "We shall see the Teacher," came to Jetavana, worshipped the Teacher, and saw the eighty great Elders. Wandering about the monastery, they came to the dwelling-place of the Elder Cakkhupāla, and thinking "We shall see him too," turned toward it in the evening. At that moment a great cloud arose; thinking "Now it is evening and a cloud has also come up — we shall go and see him in the morning," they turned back. The rain fell during the first watch of the night, and by the middle watch it had cleared over the village. The Elder, being energetic and accustomed to walking meditation, therefore in the last watch went down to his walking-path. But because the ground was freshly wet, many small creatures (glow-worms/insects) had come out, and most of them were killed as the Elder paced up and down. The resident monks had not swept the Elder's walking-path in time. The visiting monks, thinking "We shall see the Elder's dwelling," came and saw the creatures on the walking-path, and asked, "Who walks here?" "Our preceptor, Lord." They said to their preceptor: "Look at the deed of this ascetic! While he had his sight, he used to lie down and sleep, doing nothing; but now, blind, while walking up and down, he has killed so many creatures — wishing to do good, he has done wrong."

Then they went and reported to the Tathāgata: "Lord, the Elder Cakkhupāla, while walking, has killed many creatures." "But did you see him killing them?" "We did not see it, Lord." "Just as you did not see it, so he too does not see those creatures; for those whose defilements are destroyed, there is no such thing as an intention to kill, monks." "Lord, as for his attainment of arahantship..."

89

"Given this antecedent condition, why was he born blind?" — "Through the power of his own deed." "But what did he do?" "Then, monks, listen: In the past, in the kingdom of King Báráṇasi, while the kingdom was being ruled, there was a physician who traveled about from village to village, from town to town (c. -nigamame), practicing the physician's craft. Having come to one town, seeing a woman with weak eyes, he asked: 'What troubles you?' — 'I cannot see with my eyes.' — 'I will make medicine for you.' — 'Make it, sir.' — 'What will you give me?' — 'If you can make my eyes normal, I will become a slave to you together with my sons and daughters (c. -i).' He said, 'Good,' and prepared the medicine; with a single application of medicine her eyes became normal. She thought: 'I promised to become his slave together with my sons and daughters; but surely he will not come seeking affection from me (or: "sineham"?); I shall deceive him.' So when the physician came to her, she was asked, 'How are you, good lady?' and she said, 'Before, my eyes only ached a little, but now they ache even more.' The physician thought: 'This woman is trying to deceive me and does not wish to give me anything; I have no use for the wages she would give; now I shall make her blind.' Having thought this, he went home and told his wife the matter; she remained silent. He then prepared a medicine, went to the woman's presence, and said, 'Good lady, apply this medicine,' and had her apply it; both her eyes were extinguished like lamp-flames going out.

"Monks, that physician was Cakkhupāla. Then, the deed done by my son followed after him, step by step; indeed, an evil deed follows after the doer, just as a wheel follows the hoof-print of the ox pulling the yoke." Having related this story and having joined the connection, the Dhamma-king, like one stamping with the royal seal upon the foundation thus laid down, spoke this verse:

"Mind precedes all things, mind is their chief, they are mind-made;
if one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind,
then suffering follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the draft-ox."

Herein, "mind" means all consciousness belonging to the four planes, beginning with the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere. But in this particular passage, what is meant, by way of being fixed, determined, and delimited through its arising in that physician at that time, is specifically the consciousness accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion.

90

"Pubbaṅgamā" (forerunner) means: having been the first to go, [it is] accompanied [by the rest].

"Dhammā" means the four kinds of dhamma according to the categories of quality, teaching, scripture, and non-being. Among these, dhamma and adhamma are neither of the same nor of different results: "adhamma leads to hell" (var. "leads to hell"), "dhamma leads to a good destination" (var. reading) — this is called quality-dhamma (guṇadhamma). "I will teach you the dhamma that is good in the beginning" — this is called teaching-dhamma (desanādhamma). "Here, monks, some sons of good family learn the dhamma — the sutta, the geyya" (var. reading) — this is called scripture-dhamma (pariyattidhamma). "At that time there are no dhammas" (var. reading), "there are aggregates" (var. reading) — this is called non-being-dhamma (nissattadhamma), also termed non-living-dhamma (nijjīvadhamma) — it is the same thing. Among these, it is the non-being, non-living dhamma that is intended here; in its essential nature it consists of the three formless aggregates: the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations — these indeed are the "mind-forerunners" (manopubbaṅgamā).

How is it that mind is their forerunner? Because, arising together with these at one and the same time, having the same basis and the same object, not preceding them but arising simultaneously, it is called "forerunner" in the sense of being the condition for their arising. Just as, among many people jointly committing acts such as the plunder of a village, when asked "who is their forerunner?" — the one who is their leader, on whom they depend in carrying out that deed, whether he be restrained (var. "given") or reckless, he is called their forerunner — in just this way the matter here should be understood. Thus, in the sense of being the condition for arising, mind is the forerunner of these [mental factors], hence "mind-forerunners" (manopubbaṅgamā); for these cannot arise without mind arising (var. "without mind being produced"), whereas mind can arise even when certain mental concomitants do not arise.

But in the sense of being the chief/ruling factor, mind is foremost among these, hence "mind-foremost" (manoseṭṭhā) — just as among thieves and the like, the chief of thieves and such are the rulers, the foremost, so too mind is foremost among these [mental factors] (var. reading). And just as things made of wood and so forth are called "wooden-made" and the like, so too these [mental states], being produced from mind, are called "mind-made" (manomayā).

"Corrupted" (paduṭṭhena) means defiled by adventitious defilements such as covetousness and so on (var. reading); for the natural mind becomes defiled by the taints of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and it is not that the mind [itself, as it was] before [the defilement] —

...the mind itself (?), then the Blessed One said: "This mind, monks, is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements" — thus it was said. If a person speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, then, when speaking, he thereby commits the fourfold verbal misconduct; when acting, he commits the threefold bodily misconduct; and even when not speaking or acting, through a mind corrupted by covetousness and the rest, he fulfills the threefold mental misconduct. Thus for him the ten courses of unwholesome action come to completion.

"Then suffering follows him" means: from that threefold misconduct, suffering follows that person. Owing to the power of his bad conduct, whether he goes to the four states of misery or to a similar condition among human beings, bodily and mental resultant suffering follows him in this manner — just as, for example, the wheel follows the foot of the one who draws it, or as the wheel follows the shoulder of an ox yoked and drawing its burden. Just as that ox, drawing for one day, two days, five days, ten days, even half a month, is unable to turn back the wheel or cast it off — and as it moves forward the yoke chafes its neck (or hide), and as it moves backward the wheel bruises its thigh-flesh, so that by these two means the wheel continually afflicts it and clings to its feet — in just the same way, a person who, with a corrupted mind, has fulfilled the three kinds of misconduct is, wherever he is reborn — in hell and elsewhere — followed by bodily and mental suffering rooted in that misconduct.

At the conclusion of the verse, thirty thousand monks, together with those possessing the analytical knowledges, attained arahantship, and the teaching proved beneficial also to the assembled multitude. Thus ends the story of the Elder Cakkhupala.


If there is anything of help in that story for interpreting the verse, it must be sought from what follows, which for that reason I shall now translate. After it has been related above how Cakkhupala, performing his duties with the greatest zeal, was deprived of the light of his eyes, the narrative continues thus (the monks ask, p. 89, line 2): "Lord, having attained the blessed state of an arahant, why did Cakkhupala become blind?" — "Because of his own deed," said the Teacher.

92

What then was done by him? — Listen then, O bhikkhus. Once when king Báránasi was reigning, a certain physician, traveling through the countryside and towns in pursuit of his profession, came upon a woman suffering from an eye ailment and asked her: What troubles you? — I cannot see with my eyes. — I will prepare a remedy for you. — Prepare it, sir. — What will you give me? — If you can restore my eyes to health, I will become your slave along with my sons and daughters. — Very well, he said. He prepared the remedy; with this one remedy her eyes were made well. She thought to herself: I promised that I and my sons and daughters would become his slaves... I shall deceive him. Then, when asked by the physician on his next visit how she was doing, she said: Before, my eyes hurt a little, but now they hurt worse. The physician thought: She is eager to give me nothing, having deceived me, nor will I have any benefit of the wage agreed upon with her; therefore I will now make her blind. Having pondered this with himself, he went home and told his wife about the matter. She kept silent. He, having prepared the remedy, came near to the woman and ordered this medicine to be applied. Then both her eyes were extinguished like the light of a lamp. The physician was Cakkhupála, O bhikkhus. This deed, done by my son at that time, clung to him perpetually; for an evil deed follows a man, just as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the yoke." — From this it appears that, as regards the relationship between "mind" and "dhamma," although it occupies the primary place in the verse, no light at all is shed by the story.

As for "dhamma," although the notion of the word is difficult to define in its full scope, in the first two verses and in verse 279 it is undoubtedly used in the sense of the nature and condition of human life. But the fact that the commentator, with reference to verses 1 and 2, interpreted the word as referring to the "three," and with reference to verse 279 as referring to the "five attributes" (khandhá, cf. Burnouf: Introd. p. 475, 511, 684) of human nature — this must be traced back to scholastic doctrine, and does not fit this passage at all. Gogerly, according to Spence Hardy: Eastern Monachism p. 28, [renders/interprets] this verse thus...

98

turns [the sense]: "Mind precedes action. The motive is chief: actions
proceed from mind. If any one speaks or acts from a corrupt
mind, suffering will follow the action, as the wheel follows
the lifted foot of the ox." He therefore understands "dhamma" as
action, which certainly cannot be the case.

The choriambus of the third foot in these two verses (bhásati vá)
and in verse 382 (yuñjati buddh-), being contrary to the authority of
the Sanskrit grammarians (cf. Boehtlingk's Chrestomathy, p. 447),
should be removed if, by analogy with verse 68 etc., we read
bhásatí and yuñjatí.


v. 2. The second verse also was spoken at Sávatthi
concerning Maddhakundalí. At Sávatthi, it is said, there was
a brahmin named Adinnapubbaka; because he had never given anything to anyone
(something not given?), he came to be known precisely as Adinnapubbaka ("Never-given-before"); he
had one son, dear and beloved; wishing to have
ornaments made for him, [thinking] "if I ask a goldsmith to make them,
a fee will have to be given," he himself
melted gold and made a pair of earrings
and gave them [to his son]; so his son came to be known precisely as
Maddhakundalí ("Soft-earring"). When the boy reached sixteen years of age,
jaundice arose in him; his mother, looking at her son,
said to the brahmin, "A disease has arisen in our son,
have him treated"; he said, "My dear, if I bring a physician,
a fee for food and payment will have to be given, and you
will see my wealth diminished"; "Well then, what will you do, brahmin?"
"I will act in such a way that my wealth is not diminished"; so he went
to the physicians and asked, "What medicine do you use
for such-and-such a disease?"; and they told him this or that remedy
involving trees and the like (-tac-?); he brought that
and prepared the medicine for his son,
but while he was doing so the disease grew stronger,
becoming incurable; the brahmin, realizing his son's weakened state,
summoned a physician, who, after examining him, said "I have some business
to attend to; summon another
physician to treat him," and having refused, departed;
the brahmin, knowing the time of his son's death had come, for the sake of seeing him...

95

Having entered for alms and gone gradually to the door of the brahmin's house, at that moment Maddhakundala was lying facing inward in the house; the Teacher, knowing the state of not being seen [by him], released one ray; the young man, [thinking] "what is this light?", turned over, and lying there, having seen the Teacher, reflecting on the blind, foolish father, [in such a way] approached the Buddha, but was unable to perform a bodily act of homage or to speak dharma or to hear it; "now even my hands are unable [to be used]; nothing else is to be done," [thinking thus] he calmed his mind with faith alone. The Teacher thought "This much is enough for him" and departed; he, not letting the Tathagata out of the range of his eyesight, letting him go, letting him go, yet remaining devoted, died and, like one freshly awakened from sleep, was reborn in the heaven-world, in a golden mansion thirty leagues [wide]. The brahmin, too, having cremated his body, gave himself up to lamentation at the cremation ground; day after day he went to the cremation ground and wept: "Where, my only son, where, my only son?" The young deity too, looking at his own fortune, considering "by what deed was this obtained?", and understanding through the Teacher's power that it was through the serenity of mind [toward him], [thought]: "this brahmin, without having given medicine to me at my time of discomfort, now goes to the cremation ground and weeps; this will lead to his breakdown, I must do something about it." So Maddhakundali, in his [deva] form, approached, and not far from the cremation ground, stood weeping with arms raised; the brahmin, seeing him, [thought] "I am weeping out of grief for my son; why is this one weeping? I will ask him" — and asking, he spoke this verse:

"Adorned, Maddhakundali,
wearing garlands, bearing the scent of sandalwood,
you cry with arms raised —
why are you distressed in the midst of the forest?"

He said: "A golden, radiant chariot-frame has arisen for me; I cannot find its pair of wheels; through that suffering I shall give up my life." Then the brahmin said to him: "Whether golden, bejeweled, made of copper (or iron?), or made of silver, tell me, good young man; I shall obtain for you the pair of wheels." Hearing this, the young man [thought]: "This one, without giving medicine to his own son, now, having failed [his son, seeks] to provide him a substitute..."

96

(c. -rúpākaṁ) Having seen him weeping, he says: "I am making a chariot-wheel out of golden material (or similar)." Let it be, [thought the brahmin], "I will restrain him," and having thought this, he said, "How large a pair of wheels will you make for me?" When told "As large as you wish," he said, "My business is with the sun and moon; give them to me." So pleading, the young man was told by him: "The sun and moon, sir, are both my brothers; my chariot is made of gold; with that pair of wheels it will shine."

Then the brahmin said to him: "You are a fool, young man, you who desire what cannot be desired; I think you will die, for you shall not obtain the sun and moon." Then the young man said: "Now, as for the matter of what can and cannot be known, is one who weeps foolish or not? Both coming and going are seen; the character of colors applies to both equally (?); but one who is dead, being black-colored, is not seen here anymore. The one weeping for that is more foolish." Hearing this, the brahmin, considering that he had spoken rightly, replying: "Truly, young man, what you say is true; indeed I who weep over the dead am more foolish, like a boy crying for the moon, wishing for one who has gone to blackness (death)." Having said this, and having become free of sorrow through the young man's words, praising him, he spoke these verses:

    "Though I was burning, as if soaked in ghee and set ablaze,
    you have extinguished my whole burning belly as if with water.
    You have drawn out my dart, my sorrow rooted in the heart;
    you who removed my sorrow have dispelled my grief for my son.
    I have had the dart drawn out, I am become cool, extinguished;
    I do not grieve, I do not weep, having heard you, young man."

Then, asking him, "Who are you?":
    "Are you a deity, a gandharva, or Sakka, lord of the gods?
    Or who are you, whose son are you? How may we know you, sir?"
he said.

Then the young man explained to him: "Having yourself laid your son on the funeral pyre, for whom you weep and lament, and having performed [this] virtuous act, I have reached the fellowship of the thirty gods." The brahmin said: "Whether little or much, we have never seen one who, giving gifts in his own house..."

97

...the observance of the uposatha, or whatever similar act, by this same deed you have gone (c. come) to the heaven-world. The young man said: "Being afflicted, suffering, grievously ill, in a wretched state in my own dwelling, I saw the Buddha, free from passion, who had crossed over doubt, the Well-farer, incomparable; joyful and with a believing mind I made añjali (salutation) to the Tathágata. By that (or: by that wholesome deed, having done [it]?) I attained companionship with the Thirty [gods]." While he was speaking thus, the brahmin's whole body became filled with joy, and expressing that joy he said: "Wonderful, marvelous indeed, such is the fruit of an act of mere salutation! I too, joyful and with believing mind, this very day go for refuge to the Buddha." He said this (c. said). Then the young man [said] to him:

    "This very day I go for refuge to the Buddha,
    and to the Dhamma and Saṅgha, with a believing mind.
    Likewise take up the five precepts of training,
    unbroken and complete:
    Refrain quickly from taking life,
    avoid taking what is not given in the world,
    do not drink intoxicants, do not speak falsehood,
    and be content with your own wife," he said.

He, saying "Good," accepted this, and spoke these verses:

    "You wish me well, O spirit, you wish me good, O deity;
    I will do as you say, you are my teacher.
    I go for refuge to the Buddha, and to the unsurpassed Dhamma,
    and to the Saṅgha; I go for refuge, I, to the lord of gods and men.
    I refrain quickly from taking life,
    I avoid taking what is not given in the world,
    I do not drink intoxicants, nor do I speak falsehood,
    and I am content with my own wife."

Then the young deity [said] to him: "In the brahmin's house there is much wealth; approach the Teacher, give gifts, listen to the Dhamma,..."

99

Having ascended his celestial mansion, he worshipped the Teacher and stood to one side. Then the Teacher, wishing to ask him what deed he had done to obtain this attainment, spoke:

"O deity, who stand here with such surpassing beauty,
illuminating all quarters like a bright star among herbs,
I ask you, O glorious goddess:
what merit did you perform when you were a human being?"

Having spoken this verse, the young deity said: "Venerable sir, it was by gaining faith in you that I obtained this." [The Teacher asked:] "Was it by gaining faith in me that you obtained it?" [He replied:] "Yes, venerable sir." The great multitude, looking at the young deity, declared with astonishment and joy: "Oh, the virtues of the Buddha! The son of the brahmin named Adinnapubbaka, without having done any other meritorious deed, simply by gaining faith in the Teacher, attained such a glorious state!" Then the Dhamma-king, as though establishing a seal of royal authority upon a just-founded kingdom, having told this story and connected it with its context—namely that mind is the forerunner, mind is chief in doing both wholesome and unwholesome deeds, and that a deed done with a pure mind follows the person going to the heavenly or human world like a shadow that never departs—spoke this verse: "Mind precedes," etc. Here "mind" is said generally to refer to all consciousness belonging to the four planes; but in this particular passage... only consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge is to be understood; ... "dhammá" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling; ... "pasannená" (with a pure mind) means with a mind made pure by qualities such as freedom from covetousness, etc. At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma. The young deity Maddhakuṇḍalī was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and likewise the brahmin Adinnapubbaka. Thus far the greatness of this glory was spread abroad within the Buddha's dispensation. [Here ends] the Story of Maddhakuṇḍalī.

Both this story and the preceding one, like others, appear to have been transcribed from some work composed in verse—namely, of the kind called "puráṇa" (ancient narrative)—whose remnants are preserved, along with verses interspersed throughout the stories that betray their antiquity by their language, and fragments of meter marked by certain traces of rhythm.

"Tattha na hi verená" means: just as, in a place soiled with filth such as play-dirt, mucus and the like (c. -lamsi-), one who washes away the filth with more filth (eva asucihi dhovanto) is unable to make it clean and free of stench (c. -konti); indeed that place then becomes even more unclean and more foul-smelling. In just the same way, one who answers abuse with abuse, who strikes back at one who strikes, who retaliates against one who retaliates, is unable to settle enmity with enmity — rather, he only increases the enmity further... But just as those dirty things, when washed with clean water (c. ddho-), vanish, and that place becomes clean and free of stench, so too, through non-enmity — through the water of patience and loving-kindness, through wise attention, through right reflection — enmities are settled, calmed, and come to cease to exist; this is the eternal Dhamma — that is, this ancient Dhamma, consisting in the settling of enmity through non-enmity, which is the path walked by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants.

v. 6. "The others do not understand..." — The Teacher gave this
teaching while dwelling at Jetavana, with reference to the monks of
Kosambi.

In Kosambi, at the Ghositárama monastery, with five hundred
companions, there dwelt two monks: one an expert in the Vinaya
(monastic discipline) and one a preacher of the Dhamma
(Dhammakathika). One day the Dhammakathika, having made his
ablutions, left the remaining rinse-water in a vessel after setting it
down, and went away. Afterward the Vinaya-expert, entering there,
saw that water, came out, and asked the other: "Friend, was this
water left there by you?" — "Yes, friend." — "But do you know that
there is an offense in this?" — "I do not know, friend." — "Friend,
there is indeed an offense here." — "Then I will make amends for
it." — "But friend, if it was done unintentionally and without
awareness, there is no offense." So he held the view that there was
no offense in his act.

The Vinaya-expert then told his own pupils: "This Dhammakathika,
though committing an offense, does not even know that he has
committed one." Having heard this, his pupils, upon meeting the
other monk's followers, said: "Your teacher, having committed an
offense, does not know that it is an offense." They went and reported
this to their own teacher (the Dhammakathika). He then said: "The
Vinaya-expert first said there was no offense, and now says there
is one — he is a liar." They in turn went and said: "Your teacher is
a liar," and thus increased the quarrel between them.

Then the Vinaya-expert, finding his opportunity, performed the
act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) against the Dhammakathika
for his offense. From then on, even their lay supporters and
attendants split into two groups; the monks who received
instruction, the nuns, the guardian deities, the spirits friendly to
them, the sky-dwelling deities, up to the Brahma-world — all these
ordinary beings became divided into two factions. From the realm
of the Four Great Kings up to the Akanittha heaven, this uproar
spread. Then a certain monk approached the Tathágata and said:
"This act of suspension is being carried out rightfully, according to
rule, by this group..."

Suspended, suspended by unlawful procedure at the hands of those who followed the suspension — "thus suspended" — though restrained by those who had lifted the suspension, he nevertheless, without reconciling himself with them, announced that he continued to go about as before (—?). It is said that the Lord, having twice sent word asking whether they wished to become reconciled, and having heard "Venerable sir, we do not wish to become reconciled," heard on the third occasion that the Order of monks was divided — "the Order of monks is divided" — and went to their presence. He pointed out to the suspending monks the danger of (wrongful) suspension, and to the others the danger of not acknowledging an offence; and he further instructed them that, within that very boundary, having permitted the Uposatha and other observances to be performed in common, they should sit down without separation at meals and on other occasions. But hearing that they continued to live with their disputes unresolved, he went there and said, "Enough, monks, do not have disputes," and so on, declaring: "Monks, these things — quarrel, strife, contention, dispute — bring no benefit; relying on a quarrel, even the little quail brought about the death of the elephant Hatthinaga" — and he told the Latukika Jataka. "Monks, live in concord, do not dispute; relying on dispute, many thousands of carpenters met their death" — and he told the Vaddhaka (Carpenters') Jataka. Yet even so, when they did not heed these words, a certain monk who spoke rightly, not wishing to trouble the Tathagata, said: "Let the Lord come, venerable sir; let the Lord, master of the Dhamma, remain unconcerned; let the Lord dwell devoted to a pleasant abiding here and now; we ourselves shall become known on account of this quarrel, strife, contention, and dispute." When this was said, he related: "Monks, once upon a time in Baranasi there was a king of Kasi named Brahmadatta" — and so told how Brahmadatta, having seized the kingdom of King Dighiti of Kosala, caused him, who was living in disguise as an unknown man, to be put to death; and how Dighavu-kumara, when his own life was spared, from that time onward brought about reconciliation between them. Having told this, he said: "Monks, such patience and gentleness as this should exist even toward kings who have taken what was not given to them; so too here, monks — having gone forth as monks under this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline, you ought to be patient and gentle." But even having admonished them thus, he was unable to bring them to reconciliation. Being troubled by that crowded dwelling-place, he grew weary, thinking: "Now I dwell here in discomfort amid the crowd, and these monks do not follow my word; what if I..."

...would dwell [there]. Then that elephant king, leaving the herd, went to where the Blessed One was, to the foot of the Bhaddasâla tree in the forest grove protected for Pârileyyaka (var. -kamra-). Having approached and worshipped the Blessed One, looking around and seeing nothing else [to do], striking the foot of the Bhaddasâla tree with his foot, he broke off a branch with his trunk and swept the place clean. From then on, he would take a water-pot with his trunk and prepare drinking water and water for washing; when there was need for hot water, he would prepare hot water in this manner: rubbing sticks together with his trunk, he would produce fire (var. -i), kindle it; lifting up the pieces of wood (var. -e) and setting them alight, he would heat stones here and there, roll them along with a wooden pole, and, having separated them, throw them into a small hollow (?). Then, taking down his trunk and perceiving that the water had become hot, he would go to the Teacher and pay homage; the Teacher, saying "the water is heated, Pârileyyaka," would go there and bathe. Then the elephant would bring him various kinds of fruit and give them to him.

When the Teacher went into the village for alms, the elephant would take the Teacher's bowl and robe, place them upon a mound, and go along together with the Teacher. When the Teacher reached the outskirts of the village, he would say: "Pârileyyaka, it is not possible to go further than this; bring me my bowl and robe." Having had them brought to him, he would enter the village. The elephant, too, would stand right there until the Teacher came out again, and at the time of the Teacher's return, having gone forward to meet him, would take the bowl and robe as before, bring them down at the dwelling place, and, having performed this duty, would fan the Teacher with a branch. At night, in order to ward off attacks by wild beasts, he would take up a great club with his trunk, thinking "I will guard the Teacher," and would patrol back and forth through the forest grove until sunrise. It is said that from that time onward, this forest grove came to be called "Rakkhitavanasanda" (the Protected Forest).

At sunrise (var. -o), having brought water for rinsing the mouth (var. -he), he performed all his duties by this same method. Then a certain monkey, rising up, seeing that elephant (var. -i) performing proper service for the Tathâgata, thought, "I too will do something," and while searching about one day he found a stick with a honeycomb free of flies. Breaking off the stick, he carried the honeycomb together with the stick to the Teacher's presence; cutting a plantain leaf, he placed the honeycomb upon it and offered it. The Teacher accepted it. The monkey, watching to see whether he would actually make use of it or not, having taken note, sat down...

Having seen, wondering "what could this be?", he took up a stick with a knob, turned it over,
and on examining it saw some eggs; having seen them, he removed them to one side and offered [the branch],
and the Teacher made use of it. He, delighted in mind, took hold of that very branch
and stood swinging on it; then the branches that were not held firmly, as well as those that had been trodden,
broke. He fell upon a single stump and had his body pierced through,
and dying with a serene and confident mind, he was reborn in the Tavatimsa heaven, in a golden palace thirty leagues wide,
attended by a thousand heavenly nymphs. Meanwhile, the fact that the Tathagata
was being attended there by the elephant Hatthinaga, and the manner of his dwelling,
became known throughout all Jambudipa (variant: -bú-). Then from Savatthi city, Anathapindika,
Visakha the great laywoman, and such other great families, sent word
to the Elder Ananda in this manner (variant -han-): "Reverend sir, show us the Teacher,"
they said. Also five hundred monks who had completed the rains-retreat in various dwellings
approached the Elder Ananda [saying]: "For a long time, friend Ananda, we have longed
to hear the Blessed One's Dhamma-talk face to face; it would be good, friend Ananda, if we
could obtain a hearing of the Lord's Dhamma-talk in person" — thus they requested
(variant: yám-). The elder, taking those monks, went there, thinking: "For one who dwells alone,
it would not be fitting for the Tathagata to be approached by so many (variant: etth-) monks at once";
thinking thus, he left those monks outside and approached the Teacher alone.
The monkey (Parileyyaka), seeing him, took up a stick and ran forward. The Teacher, looking on, said:
"Go away, Parileyyaka, do not do that (or: do not drive him away) — this one is an attendant of the Buddha," he said. At that,
the monkey threw down the stick right there, and asked about taking the bowl and robe; the elder did not
give them to him, thinking: "If I become one of grasping disposition (-hita-?),
I will not place the Lord's requisites upon the stone slab meant for sitting (-essatíti?)" —
thinking thus, the elder set the bowl and robe down upon the ground. For those of proper conduct
do not place their own belongings upon the seat or bed of their teachers.
The elder, having paid homage to the Teacher, sat down to one side. The Teacher,
having asked, "Did you come alone?" and having heard that he had come together with five hundred

he said, "Call them in"; and the elder did so.
The Teacher, having exchanged friendly greetings with them, said to those monks:
"Reverend sirs, the Blessed One is delicate in body, and you..."

In this form the Pali and Sanskrit languages have taken over something from each other: for the sound "s" in the verbal suffix "mase" (from "masai," a form amplified from the Vedic "masi") the Pali language has preserved, while Sanskrit indeed converts it into "h." Verses 7-8. Location: Setavyanagara. Characters: Cūḷakāla and Mahākāla.

There, "subhānupassī" (variant reading: -siti) means "dwelling while regarding as pleasant" — that is, having abandoned the mind to attractive objects. For whatever person, seizing upon signs and particulars (variant: anubyañj-), grasps at things thinking "the nails are beautiful," grasps thinking "the fingers are beautiful," and likewise grasps as beautiful the hands, feet, calves, thighs, hips(?), belly, breasts, neck, lips, teeth, mouth, nose, eyes, eyebrows, eyelashes, forehead, hair; grasps thinking "the hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin are beautiful"; grasps thinking "the color, the beauty, the shape are lovely" — such a person is called "subhānupassī," "one who regards as pleasant"; thus [the phrase means] one dwelling while so regarding things as pleasant. ... "Kusītaṁ" [means lazy] through being under the sway of thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty. "Hīnavīriyaṁ" means devoid of energy, lacking exertion of effort in the four postures. "Pasahati" means overpowers, overwhelms. "Like the wind [overpowering] a weak tree" — meaning like a weak tree grown on broken ground, [overcome] by a strong wind; just as that wind causes the tree's flowers and fruits and so forth to fall, breaks even its small branches, and uproots the whole tree together with its roots, felling it and making it go with roots upward and branches downward — in just this way, the Māra of defilements that has arisen within overpowers such a person... "Asubhānupassī" means regarding as unattractive one of the ten kinds [of foulness], applying the mind to what is repulsive — regarding the hair as unattractive, regarding the body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, color, and shape as unattractive. "Indriyesu" means in the six sense faculties, being well restrained, free from grasping at signs and so on, with the doors [of the senses] shut...

As for "amattaññuṁ," it should perhaps be read as "c'amatta-," compare verse 191 "c'attha-," verse 41 "vat'ayaṁ," verse 77 "ovadeyy'anus-," verse 826 "ajj'ahaṁ."

...attains no state, no prosperity of wealth. One who neither gives himself nor causes another to give — he, in whatever existence he is reborn, does not obtain even a mouthful of rice-gruel to fill his belly; he is without protector, without support. But one who himself gives and also causes another to give — he, in whatever existence he is reborn, in a hundred existences, in a thousand existences, in a hundred thousand existences, obtains both prosperity of wealth and prosperity of retinue. Thus he taught the Dhamma.

Having heard this, a certain wise man thought: "Indeed wonderful, sir, is the reason given in this teaching of the Dhamma! I ought to perform the deed that produces these two kinds of success." Thinking thus, he invited the elder: "Venerable sir, tomorrow please accept alms-food from me."

[The elder asked:] "How many monks do you need, lay devotee?" "But how large is your retinue, venerable sir?" "A thousand, lay devotee." "Then please accept alms-food tomorrow together with all of them, venerable sir." The elder consented.

The lay devotee, walking through the streets of the town, said: "Good people, I have invited a thousand monks; how many monks' food can each of you provide?" — thus urging them on, asking each, "How many will you give for?"

The people, each according to his own means, said: "We will give for two," "We for twenty," "We for a hundred."

The lay devotee said: "Then let us gather in one place and cook together; bring all the sesame, rice, ghee, molasses and so forth" — and so he had everything brought together in one place.

Then a certain householder gave him a perfumed ochre robe worth a thousand coins, saying: "If your fund for giving is insufficient, sell this and complete the gift; but if it is sufficient, give it to whichever monk you wish." His whole fund for the gift proved sufficient, and nothing at all was lacking.

So he asked the people: "This ochre robe, given by a certain householder with such instructions, has become surplus — to whom shall we give it?"

Some said: "To the Elder Sāriputta." Others said: "The elder who comes at harvest time, who is always on the move, Devadatta, our companion in all our happy and unhappy occasions, ever present like a water-jar — let us give it to him."

When a count was taken, those who said it should be given to Devadatta turned out to be the majority — four times as many. Then him...
