They gave [it] to Devadatta; he, having cut it, having re-made it, having girded himself with it, covered himself and went about; having seen this [they said]: "This is not fitting for Devadatta, it is fitting for the Elder Sáriputta, it is fitting for the Elder Sáriputta" (variant: -ko) [or] "Devadatta, wearing and covering himself with what is unfitting for himself, goes about" — thus they said. Then a certain monk dwelling in the countryside, having gone from Rájagaha (variant: -ha) to Sávatthi, having paid homage to the Teacher, and having had a friendly greeting exchanged [with him] (variant: -tthá-), being asked by the Teacher about the comfortable dwelling of the two chief disciples (add: "then"), from that point on related the whole matter. The Teacher [said]: "Monks, it is not only now that this one wears a garment unfitting for himself; formerly too he wore [such a garment]" — having said this, he related a story of the past: "In the past, in Báránasi, while Brahmadatta was reigning, there lived in Báránasi (variant: -si) an elephant-hunter who used to kill elephants (variant: -i), and having taken the tusks, the claws, the entrails, and the thick flesh, sold them and so made his living. Then in a certain forest, many thousands of elephants (variant: -i), going out to pasture, having seen Pacceka Buddhas, from that time onward, while going along, at the time of going would fall upon their knees (variant: jann-), pay homage, and then depart. One day the elephant-hunter, seeing this behavior, [thought]: 'I kill these with difficulty, and yet these, at the time of coming and going, pay homage to Pacceka Buddhas — I wonder, having seen what, they pay homage thus,' and reflecting, he noticed the yellow robe, and thought: 'Now, if I obtain a yellow robe, I shall prosper.' Having thought this, he went down into the pool of a certain Pacceka Buddha who was bathing, and while [the robes] were placed on the bank, he stole a robe from among those placed there, and on the path by which those elephants came and going, having taken a spear, he covered his head and body with it and sat down. The elephants, seeing him, took him to be a Pacceka Buddha, paid homage (variant: saṁññásaya), and departed. He then struck with his spear the one going last among all of them (variant: sabba), killed it, took the tusks and so forth, and buried the rest in the ground (variant: -ni-), and went away. Later on, the Bodhisatta, having taken rebirth in the womb of an elephant, became the chief of the elephant herd, their leader (variant: -tí); even then, this same thing happened. The Great Being, learning of the diminishing of his retinue (variant: -niṁ), asked: 'Where have these elephants (variant: -i) gone, that they have become few?' Being told, 'We do not know, lord,' [he thought]: 'Whatever troop goes anywhere, I...'

They would not go without asking leave, thinking, "I must be on watch here, because of danger from brigands at this spot." Having put on the ochre robe there, he reflected, suspecting, "Since he is sitting near by, there must be some watch kept against brigands." Wishing to seize that one, he sent all the elephants ahead and himself came along behind, lagging. Having bowed to the rest of the elephants as they went by, he saw the Great Being approaching; furling his robe, he readied his spear. The Great Being, keeping mindfulness established, as he came on, stepped back and dodged the spear. Then, thinking, "Now he will destroy this elephant," he rushed forward to seize him. The other put a tree before himself and hid behind it. Then, encircling him together with the tree with his trunk, intending to seize him and dash him to the ground, when he pulled him forth he saw the ochre robe displayed by him, and thought: "Shall I tear this? Surely there would be shame for me before the many thousands of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and arahants free of taints." So, forbearing, he asked him, "How many elephants have you destroyed with this robe?" When told, "Yes, friend, so many," he said: "Why have you done such a cruel deed — wearing a garment unsuited to yourself, one suited only to those free of passion, and committing such an act?" Having said this, he rebuked him further: "One not free from stains..." and so on, "...he indeed deserves the ochre robe" — and said, "What you have done is improper."

The Teacher, having given this Dhamma teaching, joined the Jātaka together thus: "At that time the elephant-killer was Devadatta, and the elephant-king who rebuked him was I myself" — and said: "Not only now, monks, but formerly too Devadatta wore a garment unsuited to himself" — and having said this, he spoke these verses beginning "One not free from stains..." This matter should also be illustrated by the Chaddanta Jātaka.

Herein, "not free from stains" means: being stained by such taints as passion and the rest, he will wear [the robe] by way of using it as undergarment, overgarment, or covering — "will put on" is also a reading... "whose stains are vomited" means: one whose stains have been vomited forth, cast away, and abandoned by the four paths; "in virtues" means: in the four kinds of purified virtue; "well composed" means: thoroughly settled, well established...

At the conclusion of the verses, the resident monk of that region became a stream-enterer, and many others too attained the fruits of stream-entry and so on.

...on the road being cleared for entering the city of Rammana, seeing the people [at work], he himself also took one stretch of ground; and as that place had not yet been cleared by the time the Teacher arrived there, having made himself a bridge over the mud, he lay down, saying: "Let the Teacher, together with his community of disciples, cross over the mud by stepping on me, without stepping into the mud." The Teacher, seeing him lying there, said: "This is a Buddha-sprout; in the future, after an incalculable aeon plus a hundred thousand aeons more, he will become a Buddha named Gotama." Having received this prediction from that Teacher, he afterward received predictions from Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, Padumuttara, Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, Tissa, Phussa, Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa — having illumined the world, he obtained the prediction in the presence of these twenty-four Buddhas who had arisen. "It is time, great hero, to be conceived in a mother's womb;
Saving the world with its gods, awaken to the deathless path."

When this was said, having reviewed the five great investigations, he passed away from there and took conception in the Sakyan royal family. Cared for there amid great splendor, he in due course reached the prime of youth, and in the three mansions suited to the three seasons he enjoyed the glory of royalty as if it were heavenly splendor. One day, while going to the pleasure garden, he saw in succession the three divine messengers — manifested as old age, sickness, and death — and a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him, so he turned back. On the fourth occasion, having seen a renunciant, he thought, "Going forth is good," and conceived a liking for the renunciant life. He went to the garden and spent the day there. Is it not so that this venerable one is of great wisdom? Then why does he attain the knowledge of the limits of discipleship later than Mahāmoggallāna?

Because of the greater preliminary preparation—just as poor men, wishing to go somewhere, set out quickly at once, but for kings, the great preparation of arranging elephant-vehicles and so forth takes longer to be ready—it should be understood that the matter stands in the same way here.

"I will not grant it, dear ones." "Then, Your Majesty, let it be one month for each of us — grant three months." "Very well, dear ones; then feed him for three months."

"But, venerable sir, what did the chief disciples do?" "They made the aspiration for the state of chief disciple." Both of them were friends who had played together in the sand as children. Sarada the young man, after his father's death, having come into possession of the great wealth belonging to the family, one day went to a secluded place and thought: "I know only this present existence, not the state of existence in another world; and death is certain for all beings that are born. It would be good for me to go forth into the monastic life and seek the doctrine of liberation." He then approached his friend and said: "Friend Sirivaddhaka, I will go forth and seek the doctrine of liberation; will you be able to go forth together with me?" "I shall not be able to, friend; you alone should go forth." He thought: "There is no such thing as going to the other world taking along one's friend, relatives, or kinsmen; whatever is done is one's own alone." Then, having opened his storehouse of jewels, he gave a great donation to the poor, the destitute, beggars, and petitioners, and having gone to the foot of a mountain, went forth as an ascetic sage.

Following him, one, two, three, and so on going forth after him, there came to be as many as seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics. He, having developed the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments, taught those ascetics the preliminary practice of the kasina meditation device. They all developed the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments.

At that time the Buddha named Anomadassin arose in the world. His city was named Candavatī; his father was the noble named Yasavasanta; his mother was the queen named Yasodharā; his Bodhi tree was the ajjuna tree; Nisabha and Anoma were his two chief disciples; Varuṇa was his attendant; Sundarā and Sumanā were his two chief female disciples. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years; his body was fifty-eight cubits in height; his bodily radiance extended twelve yojanas; he had a retinue of one hundred thousand monks.

One day at dawn, having risen from the attainment of great compassion and surveying the world, he saw the ascetic Sarada and thought: "Today, because of my going to the presence of the ascetic Sarada, a great exposition of the Dhamma will take place. He will aspire to the position of chief disciple, and his friend, the householder-merchant Sirivaddha, to the position of second disciple. At the conclusion of the teaching, his retinue of seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics will attain arahantship. It would be good for me to go there." So thinking, he took his own bowl and robe, and [set out with] another [monk]...

Without telling anyone, having become solitary like a lion-cub, [the Buddha], wishing it to become known that he was indeed the Buddha just as he was being watched by Saradatapasa's pupils who had gone off in search of fruit, descended from the sky and stood firmly established on the ground before Saradatapasa. Saradatapasa, having seen the Buddha's majestic power and the perfection of his bodily form, and having reflected upon the marks [of a Great Man], thought: "One endowed with these marks, if he dwells at home in the midst of a household, becomes a king, a Wheel-turning Monarch; but if he goes forth, having removed the covering [of ignorance] from the world, he becomes an Omniscient Buddha." Having thus determined without doubt that this man was the Buddha, he went forward to meet him, paid homage with the five-point prostration, prepared a seat, and offered it. The Blessed One sat upon the seat that had been prepared. Saradatapasa too, taking a seat suitable for himself, sat down to one side.

At that time seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics, having gathered excellent and juicy fruits, arrived at their teacher's presence; and seeing the seats occupied by the Buddha and by their teacher, they said: "Teacher, we have always thought there was no one greater than you in this world; but this man seems greater than you." [The teacher replied:] "What are you saying, my children? You wish to make Mount Sineru, which rises eighty-four thousand leagues high, equal to a mustard seed! Do not, my children, ever compare me with the Omniscient Buddha!" Then those ascetics thought: "If this person were not a truly majestic and sovereign being, our teacher would not behave toward him in such a way; surely he must be very great," and all of them fell with their heads at his feet and paid homage.

Then the teacher said: "My children, we have no gift worthy of our Buddha; yet the Teacher has come here at the proper time for the alms-round, so let us give a gift according to our ability. Bring whatever excellent fruits you each have." Having had the fruits brought, he washed his hands and himself placed them in the Tathagata's bowl. The very moment the Teacher accepted the fruit, deities cast divine nourishment into it as well. That ascetic himself filtered water and offered that too.

Then, when the meal was finished and the Teacher was seated, [the hermit] summoned all his pupils and sat engaging in edifying conversation in the Teacher's presence. The Teacher thought: "Let the two chief disciples come here together with the community of monks." Having perceived the Teacher's thought...

...having arrived with their entourage of ascetics who were free from cankers, having saluted the Teacher, they stood to one side. Then the ascetic Sarada addressed his pupils: "Dear ones, there is no seat for the Buddhas, not even one fit for a hundred thousand ascetics—there is not even a low seat. Today a greater honor for the Buddha must be made ready by you; bring flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain." [Someone said:] "How could this be mere idle elaboration? For one possessed of psychic power, the range of that power is inconceivable." In a moment those ascetics, having brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance, prepared for the Buddha a flower-seat a yojana in size; for the two chief disciples, seats of three gāvutas each; for the rest of the monks, seats of half a yojana; and for the junior-most member of the Saṅgha, a seat the size of a bull's back. That in a single hermitage such great seats could be prepared in this way should not be wondered at—this is simply the range of psychic power.

When the seats had thus been prepared, the ascetic Sarada, standing before the Tathāgata with his joined palms raised, said: "Venerable sir, for my long-lasting happiness, please ascend and sit upon this flower-seat"; and having gathered together various flowers and fragrances into a single flower-seat, he spoke these words:

"This seat, O hero, is prepared, fitting for you;
gladdening my mind, sit upon this flower-seat.
For seven days and nights the Buddha sat upon the flower-seat,
gladdening my mind and delighting all beings together with the devas."

When the Teacher had thus sat down, the two chief disciples and the rest of the monks each sat on their own seat. The ascetic Sarada, taking a great flower-parasol, stood holding it over the Tathāgata's head. The Teacher, thinking, "May this honor from the matted-hair ascetics bring great fruit," entered into the attainment of cessation. Knowing that the Teacher had entered this attainment, the two chief disciples and the other monks likewise entered the attainment. The Tathāgata, having entered the attainment of cessation, sat for seven days; when the time for the pupils' alms-round came, they partook of forest roots and fruits, and for the rest of the time stood with joined palms raised toward the Buddha. The ascetic Sarada—
* [manuscript reads] nisídí.

Having passed one incalculable aeon, he saw the state of fulfillment [of the aspiration]; having seen it, he said to Saradatapasa: "This aspiration of yours will not be in vain. In the future, after the passing of one hundred thousand aeons plus one more incalculable aeon, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. His mother will be a queen named Mahamaya, his father a king named Suddhodana, his son will be named Rahula, his attendant Ananda, his second chief disciple Moggallana, and you yourself will become his chief disciple, the general of the Dhamma, named Sariputta." Having thus prophesied to the ascetic and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he then rose into the sky surrounded by the community of monks.

Saradatapasa then went to the senior monks among his own pupils and sent word to his friend, the householder Sirivaddha: "Venerable sirs, please tell my friend this: Your friend Saradatapasa has, at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassi, aspired to the position of chief disciple in the future dispensation of the Buddha Gotama; you should aspire to the position of second disciple." Having said this, the elders went ahead by one path and arrived at the door of Sirivaddha's house. Sirivaddha said, "Indeed, after a long time my noble teacher has come," and had them seated on seats while he himself sat on a lower one. His attendants asked, "Sir, are these not known to you?" [He replied,] "Indeed, friends, the Buddha Anomadassi came to our hermitage. We paid homage to him with our own effort. The Teacher taught the Dhamma to all; at the conclusion of the teaching, all except me attained arahantship and went forth as monks. Having seen the Teacher's chief disciple, the elder Nisabha, I aspired, in the future dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, to the position of chief disciple; you too should aspire, in that same dispensation, to the position of second disciple." [Sirivaddha said,] "I have no acquaintance with Buddhas, venerable sir." [They replied,] "Let speaking with the Buddhas be our concern; you should prepare a great offering of honor." Having heard these words, Sirivaddha, at the door of his own house, leveled an area the size of a royal threshing floor, spread sand over it, scattered flowers together with parched rice as a fifth offering, prepared a Buddha-seat covered with blue lotus, arranged seats for the rest of the monks as well, and made ready a great offering of honor and reverence...

In order to invite the Buddhas, he gave his promise to the ascetic Sarada. The ascetic, having taken the Order of monks headed by the Buddha, went to his dwelling. Sirivaddha too, having gone out to meet him, took the bowl from the hands of the Tathagata, led him into the pavilion, and when the Order of monks headed by the Buddha was seated on the prepared seats, he offered water for the hands, served them fine food, and at the end of the meal, having covered the Order of monks headed by the Buddha with costly garments, said: "Venerable sir, this undertaking is no small matter; in this same manner, please have compassion on us for seven days." The Teacher consented. He, continuing in that same manner, carried out a great almsgiving for seven days, and then, having worshipped the Blessed One, stood with his joined hands raised and said: "Venerable sir, my friend the ascetic Sarada aspired, saying, 'May I become the chief disciple of whatever Teacher arises'; I wish to become his second disciple." The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that this aspiration would be fulfilled, declared: "Having passed beyond this present incalculable aeon together with one hundred thousand kappas from now, you will become the second chief disciple of Gotama Buddha." Hearing the Buddha's prediction, Sirivaddha clapped his hands for joy. The Teacher, having given thanks for the meal, departed with his retinue back to the monastery just as he had come.

"This, monks, was the aspiration made then by these two sons of mine; just as they aspired, so they obtained — I do not look upon any other face (as my chief disciples)," he said. When this was spoken, the two chief disciples, worshipping the Blessed One, said: "Venerable sir, while we were still householders, we went to see the mountain-top festival, and so on up to our penetration of the fruit of stream-entry in the presence of the Elder Assaji" — and having recounted the whole of the present matter, they said: "We, venerable sir, went to the presence of our teacher, wishing to bring him to your feet; we told him of the futility of his own doctrine and explained the benefit of coming here." He replied: "Now, as for my becoming anyone's pupil — it is like water that has reached its final state; I shall not be able to live the life of a pupil under another." Having said this, they said: "Teacher, now the great multitude, carrying garlands and perfumes, will go and honor the Teacher alone; what then will become of you?" When this was said, he asked: "Now, in this world, are the wise many, or are the foolish many?" When it was answered, "The foolish are many," he said: "Well then, the wise..."

137

"The wise men will go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama; the slow,
slow ones will come into my presence; go you," having said this, he went
away [saying] "there is no coming back, reverend sir." Having heard this,
the Teacher [said]: "Monks, Sañjaya, through his own false view, grasped
the unessential as essential and the essential as unessential; but you,
having known through your own wisdom the essential as essential and the
unessential as unessential, having abandoned the unessential, have grasped
only the essential," and having said (that he would recite — c. having
recited), he spoke these verses: "Asāre" etc. Here, "In the unessential
those who think it essential" — the four conditions(?), the ten-based false
views — that dependent cause for them is [false] teaching; this is called
"unessential"; in that, "they see essence" means — the meaning is "those
with the false view"; "and in the essential they see the unessential" means —
the ten-based right views, for one of right view, the dependent cause for
[that right teaching] is [right] teaching; this is called "essential"; in that
there is no essence seen as essence — [such is] "those who see the
unessential [as essential]"; "they do not reach the essential" means — they
too, having grasped and remained fixed in that stronghold of wrong view, by
the power of thoughts of sensuality, etc., having become subject to wrong
intention, do not attain the essence of virtue, the essence of concentration,
the essence of wisdom (c. adds: the essence of liberation), the essence of
the vision of liberated knowledge, the essence of the ultimate truth, and
Nibbāna; "and they reach the essential" means — having known that very
essence consisting of virtue and so forth as "essential," and that of such a
wrong kind as "unessential, unessential" — those wise ones, having thus
grasped right vision and remained fixed in it, by the power of renunciation
and other right intentions, having become subject to right intention, reach
that essence of the aforementioned kind... At the end of the verses, many
attained the fruit of stream-entry, etc.; the teaching was beneficial to the
assembled company. [Thus is] the Story of the Chief Disciple.

Gogerly: Those who regard evil as good, or good as evil, will never attain
to excellence, but are nurtured in error. Those who know good to be good,
and evil to be evil, will attain to excellence, being nourished by truth.


v. 13-14. Place: Jetavana. Person: Nanda.

... Due to the absence of meditative development, even an undeveloped mind — passion [overcomes it]...

Gogerly: The virtuous man rejoices in this world, and he will rejoice in the next world. In both worlds he has joy; he rejoices, he exults, perceiving his own virtuous deeds.

v. 17. "He rejoices here" (idha tappati) — this teaching the Teacher gave while dwelling at Jetavana, with reference to Devadatta. The story of Devadatta, with all the Jātaka tales told concerning him from the time of his going forth up until his sinking into the earth, has been related in full; here is a summary of it: While the Teacher was dwelling near the market town of the Mallas called Anupiya, in the Anupiya mango grove, on the very day the marks [of a great being] were examined, it had been agreed by eighty thousand kinsmen households that eighty thousand sons would be born, so that whether a king or a Buddha arose, he would go about accompanied by a retinue of khattiyas. When most of these had gone forth into the monastic life, and it was seen that King Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimbila, and Devadatta — these Sakyans — had not gone forth, people thought: "We send our own sons forth, but these kinsmen of the Sakyans think otherwise, and therefore do not go forth." How did this talk arise? Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached Anuruddha and said: "Dear one, no one from our family has gone forth; either you go forth, or I will go forth." Having said this, [he waited]. Now Anuruddha was delicate and endowed with great wealth; even the word "there is none" had never been heard by him before. One day, when those six young khattiyas were playing a ball game, Anuruddha, having lost repeatedly, sent for cakes as the stake. His mother, having had cakes prepared beforehand, sent them. They ate them and played again; again and again he lost. His mother, having sent cakes three times when asked, on the fourth occasion sent the message "there are no cakes." He, never having heard the words "there is none" before, thinking it must be the name of some kind of cake, sent a messenger saying: "Bring me the cake called 'There-is-none.'" His mother then, having said "there are no cakes, but give it to him, sir," realizing that her son had never before heard the words "there is none," thought: "By this means I shall make this matter clear to him," and sent an empty golden dish...

...having unknowingly taken an empty dish, covered it, and sent it off. The deities who guarded the city thought: "When Anuruddha-Sakka, at mealtime, gave his own portion of food to the Pacceka Buddha, he said, 'May this word of mine never be heard (by anyone)' and 'May it never become known' — thus his prayer was made. If now he sees this empty dish, we shall not be able to enter the assembly of the gods; let our heads even split sevenfold." So they filled that dish with heavenly cakes. Having placed it in the middle of the serving-table, as soon as it was uncovered, the fragrance of the cakes spread and covered the whole city. As he stood there with a lump of cake just placed in his mouth, seventeen thousand (something, unclear) all around — he thought: "This is not my mother, this is not my mother; for all this time she has not cooked me cakes like this; from now on I will not eat any other cake." So he went home and asked his mother: "Mother, am I dear to you, or not dear?" "My son, you are dearer to me than my own eye, dearer than my own heart." "Then why have you not cooked cakes for me all this time, mother?" She then asked the housemaid: "Is there any cake, dear?" "The dish is full, madam; cakes like these have never been seen before." She thought: "My son must be a meritorious being, inclined toward some great attainment; the deities must have filled the dish and sent these cakes." Then the son said: "Mother, from now on I will eat no other cake; cook only this kind of cake for me." She, thinking that from then on he wished to eat cake, again unknowingly took up an empty dish, covered it, and sent it off — and this continued until he had gone through the whole house; so long did the deities keep sending cakes. He, not even understanding this much, how could he know what renunciation means? Therefore he asked his brother: "What is this thing called renunciation?" And when told: "One who has had his hair and beard shaved off, wears the ochre robe, sleeps on a leather mat or a cane bed, and lives by walking for almsfood — that is called renunciation," he replied: "Brother, I am delicate; I will not be able to go forth." "Then, dear, learn a trade and live the household life; it is not possible for even one of us not to go forth." Then who is this...

...having taken off the ornaments, having made them into a bundle [he said], "Upali, turn back; these are enough for you for a livelihood" — thus they gave them to him. He, falling at their feet and lamenting, being unable to go on ahead, turned back; at the time of their parting, the forest seemed as if weeping, as if the earth itself had become trembling.

Upali, having turned back a little, thought: "These Sakyan kinsmen are fierce; they would even kill me, thinking I have destroyed the princes. Since these very Sakyan princes have given up such splendor and cast aside these priceless ornaments as if they were a mere lump of spittle, going forth [as they are], why should I cling to this bundle of various and sundry ornaments?" So thinking, he let go of the bundle, hung those ornaments on a tree, saying "Let whoever wishes take them," and went to where the princes were. They asked him, "Why have you turned back?" He told them the reason. Then, taking him along, they went to the Teacher, [saying]: "Lord, we are Sakyans, proud of our lineage; this man has long been our attendant. Let him be ordained first; we will perform to him the duties of homage and so forth first toward him, so that our pride may be destroyed." Having said this, they had him ordained first and then were themselves ordained afterward.

Among them, the Venerable Bhaddiya, in that very same rainy season, became one possessed of the threefold knowledge. The Venerable Anuruddha, having obtained the divine eye, afterward, upon hearing the Mahāpurisavitakka Sutta, attained Arahantship. The Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The elder Bhagu and the elder Kimbila, later on, having developed insight, attained Arahantship. Devadatta attained only the mundane supernormal powers.

Later, while the Teacher was dwelling at Kosambī, great gain and honor arose for the community of disciples of the Tathāgata. People, bringing cloths, medicines, and the like, entering the monastery, would ask, going about looking at the seats of the eighty great disciples: "Where is the Teacher? Where is the elder Sāriputta? Where is Moggallāna? Where is the elder Mahākassapa? Where is the elder Bhaddiya? Where is the elder Anuruddha? Where is the elder Ānanda? Where is the elder Bhagu? Where is the elder Kimbila?" But no one, even in passing, said, "Where is the elder Devadatta sitting or standing?" He thought: "I was ordained together with these very ones; they are of royal birth who have gone forth, and I too am of royal birth who has gone forth. These people, bearing gain and honor, seek out my name..."

143

There is no (one) to grasp (that); thinking "By whom indeed, having pleased (him) together, might I produce gain and honour for myself," this occurred to him: "This king Bimbisara, at the very first sight, together with eleven nahutas (of followers), became established in the fruit of stream-entry; it is not possible to become one (in intimacy) with him through this (approach). Nor is it possible with the king of Kosala either. But this son of the king, Ajatasattu, sitting on his lap, does not know the merits or faults of a prince; through this (boy) I shall become intimate (with power)." Thinking thus, having gone from Kosambi to Rajagaha, he created by magic the form of a boy, and having wound four venomous serpents—one on each of the four limbs, one wrapped around the neck, and one made into a turban on the head, and one placed on each shoulder—he descended from the sky by means of this girdle of serpents and sat down on the lap of Ajatasattu. When asked, "Who are you?" he said, "I am Devadatta," and to dispel his fear, he dissolved that (serpent) form, and having resumed wearing the robes and bowl of a monk, he stood before him and pleased him, thus producing gain and honour for himself. Overcome by gain and honour, he generated the evil thought, "I shall take charge of the community of monks," and simultaneously with that thought's arising, he fell from his psychic power. Going to the Teacher at the Veluvana monastery, while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma to an assembly with the king present, he paid homage, and rising from his seat, with hands folded in reverence, said: "Lord, the Blessed One is now old, aged, advanced in years; let him now live at ease, devoted to dwelling in the bliss of this present existence. Let me take charge of the community of monks; hand over to me the community of monks." But the Teacher rebuked and rejected him, comparing him to spittle, saying, "Give over my monks..." Displeased, having thus for the first time conceived a grudge against the Tathagata, he departed. Then the Blessed One had an act of proclamation (of his expulsion) carried out against him in Rajagaha. Thinking, "I have now been abandoned by the ascetic Gotama; now I shall do him harm," he approached Ajatasattu and said: "In the past, princes and people lived long lives; now they have short lives. It is possible that you, while still a prince, might die (before becoming king). Therefore, kill your father and become king yourself; I shall kill the Blessed One and become the Buddha." Having said this, when that kingdom was established, he employed men to kill the Tathagata; but those men, upon reaching him, attained the fruit of stream-entry and, themselves (unable to carry out the deed), turned back...

"Having climbed up Gijjhakūṭa, I myself shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life" — so saying, he hurled down a rock, and having done the deed that drew blood (?), but being unable to kill him by this means either, he then let loose the elephant Nālāgiri. When it came, the Elder Ānanda, giving up his own life, stood in front for the Teacher's sake. The Teacher, having tamed the elephant-king, left the city, went to the monastery, and, having partaken of a great gift offered by many thousands of lay devotees, gave a graduated discourse that day to the eighteen koṭis of Rājagaha's inhabitants who had assembled, and when eighty-four thousand beings had attained realization of the Dhamma, [the monks said]: "Oh, how great are the virtues of the venerable Ānanda — that in the face of such an elephant coming he gave up his own life and stood before the Teacher!" Hearing this praise of the Elder's virtues, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, it is not only now — formerly too this one gave up his life for my sake" — and, being requested by the monks, he related the Cūlahaṁsa, Mahāhaṁsa, and Kakkaṭa Jātakas.

As for Devadatta's deeds, it was not the case (as before) that it became publicly known through the hiring of the king to kill, or the employing of assassins, or the hurling of the rock — as it became known through the release of the elephant Nālāgiri; then indeed the multitude cried out: "The king too, instigated by Devadatta alone, hired the murderer; it was through him that the rock was hurled; and now the elephant Nālāgiri has been let loose by him — taking up such wickedness, the king goes about!" Hearing this talk of the multitude, the king, having taken away the five hundred bowls of food, no longer attended upon him; and the townsfolk too gave not even almsfood to his family when they came for it. Devadatta, his gains and honors thus diminished, wishing to live by [some other] means (?), approached the Teacher and asked for the five articles [of ascetic practice]. The Blessed One refused, saying: "Enough, Devadatta — let whoever wishes be a forest-dweller." [Devadatta said:] "Whose word is more excellent, friend — the Tathāgata's or mine? I speak thus out of a wish for the stricter practice: it would be good, venerable sir, if monks were forest-dwellers for life, alms-gatherers, wearers of refuse-rag robes, dwellers at the foot of trees, and ate no fish or meat." Saying, "Let him who wishes to be freed from suffering come with me, or go," he departed. Hearing his words, some newly-ordained monks of weak understanding [thought this] a good [teaching of] Devadatta...

Having said this, [Devadatta] struck him with his knee in the middle of the chest, and hot blood at once gushed from his mouth. Then the monks, seeing the Venerable Sāriputta coming through the air surrounded by a company of monks, said: "Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta, who went forth with only one companion at the time of departure, now comes back how splendidly, with a great retinue!" The Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now that my son, coming into my presence, looks splendid thus — even when he was born in an animal womb he looked splendid when coming near me," and having said this:

"There is benefit in virtuous conduct for one devoted to hospitality:

Behold the mark of one coming, honored and surrounded by his kinsmen,
and see this other, Kāla, as if destitute of relatives" —

with this he told the Jātaka story. Again, when the monks said, "Venerable sir, it is said that Devadatta, having seated the two chief disciples on either side of him, wishing to teach the Dhamma in imitation of the Buddha's own manner, is imitating you," the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now but formerly too that he tried to imitate me, but could not succeed," and having said this:

"Look, Vīraka, at that sweetly-singing bird
resembling a peacock's neck, Savitthaka, my husband.
That bird which haunts the water's edge,
ever feeding on raw fish —
imitating him, Savitthaka
got entangled in the water-weed and died" —

having told the Jātaka beginning with these verses, on other days too, raising a similar topic, he said:

"Habitually pecking at forest trees
that are hollow and without sap,
he then came upon a Khadira tree full of heartwood,
where the hard core lay uppermost;

Your beak is shattered, your skull is split,
all your ribs are broken — now indeed, friend, how fine you look!" —

and with such verses he told these and similar Jātaka stories. Again, raising the topic "Devadatta the ungrateful," [he said]:

"We have done what was our duty, the strength that was ours we exerted; homage to thee, O king of the deer, even if we get nothing."

"This is the task of me, the blood-eater, cruel and deceiving — having come between the elephant's tusks, that he may remain there, that he may yet live" — with such verses as these he related the Jātakas. Again, concerning one who plotted for the sake of killing, with reference to the schemer, [he said]:

"This is known to the antelope, that you are sleeping in the open glade; I go to another glade, for I have no liking for this fruit" — with such verses as these he related the Jātakas. Again, when Devadatta had fallen from both — deprived of gain and honor as well as of status — as this matter was being discussed, [the Buddha] said: "Monks, this is not the first time he has fallen thus," and said:

"The eye was broken, the vessel lost, there is a witness in the house and a quarrel; both sides' work was spoiled, both the water and the fruit" — with such verses as these he related the Jātakas. Thus, while dwelling at Rājagaha, having told many Jātakas concerning Devadatta, [the Buddha] went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī and took up residence at the Jetavana monastery.

Devadatta too, in the ninth month, being ill, in his final hour wished to see the Teacher, and said to his own disciples: "I wish to see the Teacher; show him to me." When he said this, they replied: "When you were in your full strength you acted as an enemy toward the Teacher; we will not take you there." Being told this, he said: "Do not destroy me — I have borne enmity toward the Teacher, but in the Teacher there is not even so much as a hair's tip of enmity toward me. For the Blessed One has said:

'Toward Devadatta the would-be murderer, toward the bandit Aṅgulimāla, toward the elephant Dhanapāla, and toward Rāhula — everywhere his mind is the same.'"

"Show me that Blessed One," he begged again and again. So they took him up on a litter and set out. Hearing of his coming, the monks reported to the Teacher: "Lord, it is said that Devadatta is coming to see you." [The Teacher said]: "Monks, with that body he will not be able to see me." It is said that from the time he asked for the five things, the monks could no longer obtain audience with the Buddha — such is the natural course of things. Having arrived at a certain place...

148

"Venerable sir"; let him do whatever he wishes, he will not be able to see me; "Venerable sir, I have come a league from here, half a league, a gávuta, I have come near the lotus pond, venerable sir"; even if he enters inside Jetavana itself, he will not be able to see me in this way; having taken Devadatta they came to the bank of the Jetavana lotus pond, having set down the couch (c. -ni-) they descended into the lotus pond to bathe, Devadatta too, rising from the couch, placed both feet on the ground (c. bhu-) and sat down; they entered the earth, he gradually, up to the ankles, up to the knees (c. jann-), up to the hips, up to (c. yoca) the waist, up to the neck, having entered up to the chin, when he was standing in the earth up to the jawbone (c. -táká-):

"By these bones, that supreme person,
called a god among the tamers of beings between the worlds,
the all-seeing one, marked with a hundred merits,
I have gone for refuge to the Buddha with my hands" (-?)

he spoke this verse. Having seen this matter, it is said, the Tathágata ordained Devadatta; for if he had not gone forth, being a layman he would have done deeds and borne fruit, and for the sake of making conditions for the future, being unsteady (c. raddh-) he would have been unable, being steady, to stand still within a hundred leagues from the edge (inside Aví?); but having gone forth, although he will do deeds that bear fruit, he will be able to make conditions for the future — for this reason the Teacher ordained him, for after a hundred thousand aeons from now he will become a Paccekabuddha named Atthissara. He, having entered the earth, was reborn in Aví; being unsteady though the Buddha is steady, being unsteady he was unable to stand still within a hundred leagues — his body was reborn within Aví itself, of the measure of a hundred leagues in height; his head up to the neck-joint entered the upper iron shell-cap; his feet up to the ankles entered the lower earth-surface (c. -íya); an iron stake of the size of a great palm-tree trunk (c. maha-nam) came out from the western wall, pierced through the middle of the back, came out through the belly, and entered the eastern wall; another came out from the southern wall, pierced the southern side, came out through the northern side, and entered the northern wall (c. -rapahitti); another came out from the upper shell, pierced the crown, and through the lower part...

150

He told this Pingala Jataka. The monks asked the Teacher:
"Venerable sir, where has Devadatta now been reborn?"
"Monks, in the great Avici hell." "Venerable sir, after wandering here suffering,
has he then gone and been reborn again right in the place of suffering?"
"Yes, monks; whether they are ordained
or laymen, those who dwell negligently suffer in both places
alike," and having said this he spoke this verse: "Here he suffers," etc. Herein,
"he suffers here" means he suffers here through the suffering caused by his deed, amounting merely to mental distress;
"having departed" means that in the next world he suffers through the suffering of the fruit [of his deed], which is exceedingly harsh,
the suffering of the states of woe ... [This is] the story of Devadatta.

Gogerly: The sinner suffers in this world, and he will
suffer in the next world. In both worlds he suffers; he suffers,
knowing — sin has been committed by me; and dreadfully
will he suffer in the regions of torment.


Verse 18. Place: Jetavana. Person: Sumanadevi.

"... Having gone to a good destiny, for fifty-seven crores of years
and sixty hundred-thousand years, enjoying heavenly fortune in the city of Tusita,
she rejoiced exceedingly."

Gogerly: The virtuous man is happy in this world, and
he will be happy in the next world. In both worlds he is

and greatly will he rejoice in heaven.


Verses 19-20. Place: Jetavana. Persons: two companion monks.

Herein, "sahitam" is a name for the Buddha's word consisting of the Three Baskets;
having approached a teacher and learned it, reciting it much
to others, hearing that teaching and [knowing] what action [should follow]—

By what sort of person is it to be done? One who merely makes something of it is not [truly a doer] (c. ho) — like a cock's mere flapping of wings (?), right attention proceeding by way of impermanence and so on does not come about. This may be understood by the example of a cowherd hired for day-wages (c. -saṁ-): in the morning he takes charge of the cows, and in the evening, having counted them, delivers them to their owners, receiving only his day's wage; even though he wishes, he cannot enjoy the five kinds of milk-products. Just so, among pupils, the mere carrying out of duties and counter-duties is a "share" (c. -gi) that one may have, but one has no share (c. -gi) in the fruits of the ascetic life itself. Just as the milk-products of the cattle delivered by the cowherd are enjoyed by the owners themselves, so too, the persons who put the Dhamma spoken [by the teacher] into practice, proceeding according to instruction — some attain the first jhāna and so forth, others, having developed insight, attain the paths and fruits — thus it is the "owners of the cows" who truly share in the milk, that is, in the fruits of the ascetic life. Thus the Teacher spoke the first verse with reference to a monk who, though endowed with virtue and of great learning, dwells negligently and does not proceed with right attention by way of impermanence and so on; the second verse, however, was spoken with reference to a person of little learning who, nonetheless, performs his task while dwelling in right attention — spoken, that is, with reference to the practicing person. Here, "even a little" means just a small amount, perhaps the extent of one or two chapters [of the texts]. "He becomes one who lives in conformity with the Dhamma" means: having understood the meaning, having understood the Dhamma, by cultivating the preliminary practice appropriate to the supramundane Dhamma — namely the fourfold purification of virtue, ascetic practices, meditation on foulness, and so on — by living accordingly he becomes one who lives in conformity with the Dhamma. Longing for penetration, thinking "today, even today," he goes about [practicing]. Through this right practice (c. smáp-), having abandoned both lust and hatred (c. rágadveso ca), and having abandoned delusion by the right method, fully understanding the things to be understood, he becomes one whose mind is thoroughly liberated by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites, through suppression, through cutting off, through tranquilization, and through escape. "Not clinging, here or beyond" means: whether belonging to this world or the next, whether internal or external, not clinging through the four kinds of clinging to the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements — such a one, a great arahant with taints destroyed, having arrived by means of the ascetic life characterized by the path...

v. 21-23. "Vigilance is the path to the deathless" — this teaching of the Dhamma was given by the Teacher while dwelling at the Ghositárama near Kosambí, with reference to the destruction by death of the five hundred women headed by Sámávatí (c. -ti-) and the five hundred relatives (?) headed by Mágandikā. Here is the sequence of events (anupubbikathá):

In the past, in the country of Allakappa, there was a king named Allakappa, and in Vethadípa there was a king named Vethadípaka. These two, from childhood, had grown up together as friends studying a craft in the same teacher's household. After the deaths of their fathers, each raised a royal umbrella and became king of a country ten-by-ten leagues in extent. From time to time they would meet together, and sitting, standing, or lying down together, seeing the multitude of people being born and dying, they thought: "There is no one called 'one who follows after' one who is going to the next world; even one's own body must be left behind entirely — what use is there in household life? Let us go forth into renunciation." Having resolved thus, they handed over their kingdoms to their sons and wives, went forth as sage-renunciants (isi-pabbajjā), and dwelt practicing austerities in the region at the foot of the Himalayas. They considered: "We have given up our kingdoms and gone forth, yet unable to bear separation, we now live in one place — this is no different from not having gone forth at all. Therefore let us dwell separately. You stay on this mountain, I will stay on that one, and on each half-month's uposatha day we shall meet together." Then it occurred to them: "Even so, there will be too much mutual contact between us [through meeting]." So they said: "You shall light a fire on your mountain, and I will light one on mine; by that sign we shall know that each of us is alive." And so they did.

After some time, the ascetic of Vethadípa passed away and was reborn as a mighty deva-king. Then, the following half-month, when the other ascetic did not see the fire on the mountain, he thought, "My friend must have died." But the other one, at the very moment of his rebirth, surveying his heavenly glory and reflecting on the kamma [that led to it], saw that it had come about through renunciation; thinking "I shall go and see my friend who practises austerities," he gave up that divine form and, appearing as a traveler, approached him, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then the ascetic said to him: "Where have you come from?" The traveler replied: "I, venerable sir, am a traveler who has come from afar. But tell me, venerable sir, does the noble one dwell alone in this place, or is there someone else as well?" [The ascetic replied], "There is..."

"[I have] one companion," [he said]. "Where is he?" "He dwells on this mountain." "But on the uposatha day he did not light a fire; he must be dead." "Yes, venerable sir." "Yes, friend." "I am he, venerable sir." "Where were you reborn?" "I was reborn in the deva-world, venerable sir, as a mighty deva-king. But I have come wishing to see the noble one. Is there, indeed, any trouble for the noble ones dwelling in this place?" "Yes, friend, I am troubled on account of elephants." "What, venerable sir, do the elephants do?" "They drop their dung in the sweeping-place; striking with their feet they dig up the dust; so, in throwing away the dung and leveling the dust, I become weary." "Do you wish that they should not come?" "Yes, friend." "Then I shall see to it that they do not come." He gave the ascetic the elephant-charming lute and the elephant-charming spell; and in giving it, having shown the three strings of the lute, he made him learn three spells: "Striking this string, when this spell is spoken, the elephants, unable even to turn and look back, will flee." "Striking this string, when this spell is spoken, they will flee looking back behind them." "Striking this string, when this spell is spoken, the herd-leader will come forward offering his back" — having explained this, he said, "Do as you please," and departed. The ascetic, reciting the fleeing-spell and striking the fleeing-string, made the elephants flee, and so dwelt in peace.

At that time there was in Kosambi a king named Parantapa. One day, warming himself in the morning sun together with his pregnant queen, he sat upon the open terrace. The queen, having put on the king's red cloak worth a hundred thousand, sat conversing with the king, and taking from the king's finger his ring worth a hundred thousand, she put it upon her own finger. At that moment an elephant-shaped bird, passing through the sky, saw the queen and, taking her for a piece of flesh, spread its wings and swooped down. At the sound of its descent the king rose up and went into the inner chamber. The queen, being heavy with child and of a timid nature, could not move quickly. Then that bird, pouncing upon her, set her in its claw-cage and sprang up into the sky. Indeed, it is said that such birds possess the strength of five elephants...

...[the birds] would approach, and so, having carried her off through the air, [the bird] went wherever it pleased, sat down, and ate flesh there. Being carried off by it, she, terrified by fear of death, thought: "If I cry out, the human voice is a thing that startles creatures born among animals; hearing it, this bird will drop me, and thus together with my womb I shall meet my death. But in whatever place it sits down and begins to eat me, there I shall make a noise and frighten it into flying away." Through her own cleverness she endured this. Now at that time, in the region at the foot of the Himalayas, there stood a great banyan tree that had grown somewhat, spread out like a pavilion. That bird used to bring deer-like prey there and eat it. So it carried her there as well, set her down between the branches, and looked back along the path by which it had come — for it seems this looking-back at the way they came was a habit of such birds. At that moment the queen, thinking "Now I must make it fly off," raised both her hands, and making a clapping sound with her hands and a sound with her mouth, startled it into flight. Then, at the time near sunrise, the wind-forces born of karma stirred, and from every direction a thundering great cloud arose. For the queen, standing there helpless — not receiving so much as the word "Do not fear, my lady" — overwhelmed with suffering, there was no sleep for her the whole night through. At the break of day, the departure of the storm-clouds, the rising of the dawn, and her own delivery all happened at the very same moment. Taking [a name] from the cloud-season and from the dawn, she named the son that was born "Udena." Now not far from there was also the dwelling place of the ascetic Allakappa. As was his custom, during the rainy season, out of fear of the cold, he would not go into the forest for fruits; instead he would go to the foot of that [same] tree, gather bones of flesh that the birds had eaten, pound them, make a broth, and drink it. So, thinking "Today too I shall fetch bones," he went to that very spot, to the foot of the tree, and while searching for bones there, heard the sound of a child from above. Looking up, he saw the queen and said, "Who are you?" She said, "I am a human being, 'mhi' [I am]." "How did you come here?" "I was carried off by a bird with hands like talons." When this was said, he said, "Come down." She said, "I fear the confusion of castes [improper mixing]." "Who are you?" "I am a Khattiya [noble]." "I too am a Khattiya." "Then speak to me as one would to a Khattiya woman." So he spoke accordingly, and she then said, "Then let me climb down, bringing my child with me." Making a path on one side by which to climb up, he ascended, and took hold of the child, [saying] "Do not [come near] me with your hand..."

"I am the son of King Parantapa of Kosambi; the bird [called] elephant-indicator has sought me out" -- having said this (and) having told the names of the generals and others, he gave to those who did not believe: "showing this blanket and signet-ring, which belong to my father's and mother's [line], you should display [them]" -- thus speaking, he sent them off; (then) the hermit [thought]: "What should the young prince do now?" he said; "sitting on the lower branch of the tree, having spoken this spell, strike the drum; the chief elephant will come up and approach you, raising you up on his back; mounted on his back, having gone to the kingdom, you shall seize the kingdom" -- having saluted his parents, and done accordingly, having come, sitting upon the back of the elephant that had come, he whispered in its ear: "I am the son of King Parantapa of Kosambi; having taken my paternal kingdom, give it to me, lord!" -- having heard this, it trumpeted an elephant-cry [as if saying] "let many thousands of elephants assemble," and many thousands of elephants assembled; again [he said] "let the old elephants withdraw," and it trumpeted the elephant-cry, and the old elephants withdrew; again [he said] "let the too-young ones turn back," and it trumpeted, and they too turned back; then, surrounded by many thousands of warrior-elephants, having reached a border village, [he proclaimed]: "I am the king's son; those who wish for prosperity, let them come with me" -- from then on, gathering a following of men, having gone, having surrounded the city, he sent a message: "Let them give me battle or let them give me the kingdom"; the townsfolk said: "We shall not give over either [option]; our queen too, being heavy with child, was carried off by the elephant-indicator bird; we do not know whether she is alive or dead; until we hear news of her, we shall not give battle, nor the kingdom" -- at that time, it is said, the kingdom was in succession to him [i.e., to the rightful heir]; then the young prince, saying "I am her son," having told the names of the generals and others, yet to those who still did not believe, showed the blanket and the signet-ring; they, recognizing the blanket and ring, opened the gates and consecrated him to the kingdom with royal anointment. This, then, is the origin of Udena... This is the story of Ghosita the treasurer... This is the story of Sámávatí. Now, Udena had another queen named Vásuladattá, daughter of Caṇḍapajjota; in Ujjení there was a king named Caṇḍapajjota; one day, returning from the pleasure-garden, surveying his own prosperity, [he thought]: "Is there perhaps, for anyone else also..."

Such wealth as this — is this indeed the name for it? — when it was said that in Kosambi King Udena's prosperity was exceedingly great, he said: "Then we shall seize it." "It cannot be seized." "By doing whatever is needed, we shall seize it all the same." "It cannot be, sire." "Why not?" "He knows the craft called elephant-charming: tuning his instrument and playing the elephant-charming lute, he lures wild elephants and captures them. There is no one, they say, equal to him in possessing elephant-mounts; it is not possible for me to catch him." "If that is certainly so, then have a wooden elephant made and send it to a place near his border. He always goes far, whether on an elephant-mount or a horse-mount; there it should be possible to seize him when he comes." The king said, "This indeed is the method," and had a mechanical wooden elephant made, covered outside with hides, its hidden mechanism completed, and had it released near a riverbank close to the enemy's territory. Inside the elephant's belly sixty men walked back and forth; dung was brought and scattered here and there. A forest-dweller, seeing the elephant, thought, "This is a fitting one for our king," and went and reported to the king: "Your Majesty, I have seen a magnificent elephant, all white, resembling the peak of Mount Kailasa, fit for you." Udena, taking that very report as his guide, mounted his elephant and set out with his retinue. Spies, learning of his approach, went and told Candapajjota, who came and, leaving the center empty, deployed his forces on both sides. Udena, not knowing of this approach, pursued the (wooden) elephant; the men hidden within fled swiftly. As the musical-elephant (?), as though not hearing the sound of the lute whose melody the king played, kept fleeing on and on, the king, unable to catch up with the elephant, mounted a horse and pursued it. As they chased at speed, his army fell behind and the king was left alone. Then Candapajjota's men, posted on both sides, seized him and handed him over to their own king. When his army learned that he had fallen into the hands of the enemy, they made camp outside and stayed there. Candapajjota, having had Udena captured alive, had him shut up in a thief's house, with the door closed, and for three days drank the wine of victory. On the third day Udena asked the guards...

"...where is your father, the king?" she asked; "An enemy has captured me," he said, and so he drinks the victory-drink; "What sort of woman's business is this, concerning your king's affairs? Should one not capture rival kings and either release them or kill them (or let them prosper)? Having made us suffer, he drinks the victory-drink, they say!" They went and told the king of this matter; he came and asked, "Is it true that you speak thus?" "Yes, great king," he said. "Good, I will set you free; if you truly have such a mantra, show it to me." "I will gladly teach it, but only at the moment of receiving it does one learn it — will you bow to me?" he asked. "I will bow," he said — "No, I will not bow." "Then I too will not teach it." "If that is so, I will deal with you as the king sees fit." "Do as you wish; you are master of my body, but not of my mind." Having heard his bold defiance, the king thought, "How indeed shall I obtain this mantra?" Since it could not be taught to anyone else, he thought, "Let my daughter learn it in his presence, and I shall learn it from her." So he said to the man, "Will you teach it to one who bows and learns it from another?" "Yes, great king." "Well then, in our house there is a hunchbacked woman; she will sit within a curtain, and you will stand outside the curtain and recite the mantra to her." "Let her be a hunchback or a cripple, I will teach it to anyone who shows due respect." Then the king went to his daughter Vāsuladattā and said, "My dear, there is a lowly man with a shell-shaped neck who knows a priceless mantra. It cannot be taught to anyone else. You must sit within the curtain and learn the mantra; he will stand outside and recite it to you, and I will learn it from you." Thus, for fear that the two of them would become familiar with one another, he called his daughter "the hunchback" and the man "shell-neck" when speaking to each of them. The man stood outside the curtain and taught the mantra to her as she sat within. Then one day, when she had repeated the mantra's words again and again but failed to pronounce them, he said, "Hey hunchback, your mouth is too thick-cheeked to say it properly; is that how one should speak?" She grew angry and said, "You wicked shell-neck, why do you talk like that? Is a girl like me to be called a hunchback?" Lifting a corner of the curtain slightly, he said, "Who are you?" and the king's daughter replied, "My name is Vāsuladattā." "Did my father, when telling me of you, call you a hunchback?" "And when telling me of you, he likewise called you 'shell-neck.'" Then they...

Then that master, seeing the Pacceka Buddha approaching with his bowl just washed, having seen and venerated him, asked: "Venerable sir, have you received anything?" As he walked on, [he said] "We have departed, friend." The master thought: "Having been asked by me, he went away without explaining anything—so he must have received nothing." Then, looking at the bowl and seeing it empty, not knowing whether the meal at the house was finished or not, being bold yet unable [simply] to take the bowl, he said: "Venerable sir, please wait a little," and hurried home to ask, "Is our meal (finished)?" On being told it was finished, he said to his attendant: "Dear fellow, there is no one swifter than you; by swift running overtake the Reverend One, [and say] 'Give the bowl to me, venerable sir,' take the bowl and come back." At that single word, the attendant dashed off, took the bowl, and brought it back. The other, having filled it with his own food, said: "Quickly take this to the master; I will give you a share from here." He hurried off, and having given the bowl to the Pacceka Buddha, prostrating with the five points of the body touching the ground, said: "Venerable sir, time was pressing, so I went and came back with the utmost speed. By the fruit of this swiftness of mine, may vehicles capable of covering a hundred and fifty, a hundred and sixty, or a hundred and twenty yojanas be produced for me (variant: a hundred and twenty-five); and as I go and come, may my body—heated by the sun's rays—in the place of my future birth, have my command be like the sun's heat itself. In this alms-offering, the merit was given with my own hand; by the fruit of this, may you (the Pacceka Buddha), who have seen the truth, share in this merit." The Pacceka Buddha, saying "So be it," spoke:

"May all that you wish and long for be fulfilled completely,
May all your intentions be fulfilled like the full moon on the fifteenth day."

"May all that you wish and long for be fulfilled quickly,
May all your intentions be fulfilled like a wish-granting jewel."

Having spoken thus, he gave his blessing. These two verses are said to be the customary verses of thanksgiving spoken by Pacceka Buddhas. Here, "jotiraso" refers to the wish-fulfilling gem that grants all desires. This was his past conduct. He is now [reborn as] Caṇḍapajjota; by the result of that deed, these five vehicles were produced for him. Then one day the king went out to the pleasure garden for sport, [thinking] "Udena must flee today," with very large leather…

Having filled a bag with silver and gold and placed it on the back of a she-elephant, he took Vásuladattá and fled. The guards of the inner palace, seeing this, went and reported it to the king. The king quickly sent soldiers, saying "Go quickly!" Udena, knowing that the army had set out in pursuit, released and dropped the bag of coins. The people, stopping to gather up the coins, rushed on after him again. Then he released and dropped the bag of gold, and the people, delaying out of greed for the gold, fell behind; so he reached his own camp. Then, when his army saw him coming, they surrounded him and escorted him into the city. He then went and had Vásuladattá anointed, and established her in the position of chief queen. This is the story of Vásuladattá.

Now there was another woman named Mágandiyá who obtained the position of chief queen in the king's presence. She was the daughter of the brahmin Mágandiya of the Kuru country; her mother's name was also Mágandiyá, and her grandfather too was called Mágandiya. She was beautiful, comparable to a celestial nymph. Her father, unable to find a husband of suitable rank for her, when asked for her hand by great families, rebuked them, saying "You are not worthy of my daughter," and sent them away.

Then one day the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw that the brahmin Mágandiya and his wife possessed the supporting conditions for attaining the fruit of non-returning. Taking his bowl and robe, he went to their place of fire-worship in that town. The brahmin, beholding the Tathágata's form endowed with supreme beauty, thought: "In this whole world there is no other man like this man; this one is worthy of my daughter. I shall give her to him for his support," and thought further: "I have just one daughter; for this long time I have not found a man worthy of her. You are worthy of her, and she of you. Indeed, you shall gain in her a devoted attendant, and she shall prosper through gaining you as a husband. I will give her to you — please wait right here until I return," he said. The Teacher, without saying anything, remained silent. The brahmin, hurrying home, said: "Wife, wife! I have found a man worthy of our daughter! Quickly, quickly, adorn her!" Having had her adorned, he took her together with his wife, the brahmin lady, and set off to the Teacher's presence. The whole city was thrown into commotion, saying: "For so long a time..."

...having come, [the daughters of Māra] having shown an enticement arranged in the guise of maidens (var. -ri-) and the like, yet to me [said the Buddha]:

Having seen Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ratī [Māra's three daughters],
I had no desire even for sexual intercourse;
What indeed is this, full of urine and excrement,
That I would not wish to touch even with my foot?

He spoke this verse, and at the end of the verse the brahmin and the brahmin-woman were established in the fruit of non-returning. But Māgandiyā thought: "If I must admit there is no such fault in me, let it be — he treats me as mere filth and urine"; and she formed a grudge against the Teacher, [thinking], "Once I have obtained, in accordance with my birth, family, place, wealth and age, a suitable husband, I shall know what ought to be done to this ascetic." Now did the Teacher know that this ill-will had arisen in her mind, or did he not know? He did know; knowing it, why then did he speak the verse? For the sake of the other two [her parents]; for Buddhas teach the Dhamma for the sake of those who are capable of attaining the path and its fruit, without regard to resentment. Her parents took her, gave her to Cūḷamāgandiya [her uncle] in marriage, then went forth and attained arahantship. Cūḷamāgandiya too thought: "My daughter is not fit for a lowly man; she is fit only for a king" — and so he took her to Kosambi, adorned her with every ornament, and said, "This jewel of a woman is fit for Your Majesty," and gave her to King Udena. The king, seeing her, with passion suddenly arisen, conferred the consecration upon her and, having made her the head of a retinue of five hundred women (var. "of five hundred..."), established her in the rank of chief queen. Thus he came to have three chief queens, each with a retinue of one thousand five hundred dancing-women. Now at that time there were in Kosambi three merchants (setthis): Ghosita-setthi, Kukkuṭa-setthi, and Pāvāriya-setthi (var. readings noted). Before the onset of the rains-residence, they saw five hundred ascetics who had come from the Himalayas wandering for alms in the city; being pleased, they had them seated, fed them, obtained their promise [to stay], and kept them near themselves for four months. Then, when the rains were ending, having secured their promise to return, they sent them off. The ascetics thereafter spent eight months in the Himalayas and four months dwelling near them. Later, coming again from the Himalayas, they [arrived at the]...
