...having seen in that place a great banyan tree, they sat down at its foot. Among them the chief ascetic thought: "In this tree there must dwell a deity, and it will not be an insignificant one (?); here there must be a very powerful lord of devas. It would be good if he would give water to this company of seers." So saying, [the deity] gave the water. Then the ascetic thought of water for washing, and that too was given; then he thought of food, and that too was given (one manuscript adds: then he thought of food, and that too was given). Then this thought occurred to him: "This king of the devas gives everything we think of, whether we wish it or not — oh, let us see him!" So, splitting open the trunk of the tree, [the deity] showed himself. Then they said to him: "O king of devas, great is your fortune; by doing what was this obtained?" He replied, "Do not ask, sirs." "Tell us, O king of devas." Being ashamed on account of the deed he himself had done, he was unwilling to tell it; but being pressed again and again, he said, "Well then, listen," and told it as follows:

It is said that there was once a poor man who, seeking wages, got work in the household of Anāthapiṇḍika, and by that means made his living. Then one day, when the uposatha day had come, Anāthapiṇḍika, returning from the monastery, asked: "Has anyone told this workman that today is an uposatha day?" "It has not been told, master." "Then let his evening meal be cooked for him." So they cooked extra food for him. He, having worked all day in the forest, came home in the evening, and when his portion of food was served increased, thinking "I am in luck!" he ate it at once. Whereas on other days there was a great clamor in that house — "Give rice! Give soup! Give curry!" — today all was silent. He asked, "Why does no one call out?" [They answered,] "They only served your portion extra." Wondering what this could mean, he asked: "Did the rest eat?" (one version: "Did they not eat?") "For what reason?" [he asked]. "In this house, on uposatha days, no evening meal is eaten; everyone observes the uposatha, down to the infants still at the breast — their mouths are opened and the four sweet foods placed in them by the great treasurer himself, who makes them into uposatha-observers; fragrant oil lamps are lit; the small and the grown children go of their own accord and recite the thirty-two parts of the body. But we forgot to tell you about the uposatha day; therefore this food, cooked specially for you, eat it."

"If it is now proper to become an observer of the uposatha (fast-day), I too would become one," [he thought]. "Does the setthi (merchant) know this?" [they wondered]. "Then ask him," [it was said]. So they went and asked the setthi, and he spoke thus: "Having now eaten and wiped my mouth, I am going to the uposatha observance (?), resolving: 'I shall undertake the half-uposatha practice.'" The other, hearing this, did the same. Having performed the practice for the whole day, hungry as he was, winds afflicted his body; having tied a rope and taken hold of its end, he kept turning about. The setthi, hearing of this state of affairs, had the four sweet foods prepared on account of [the man's] excessive fasting, went to him, and asked: "What is it, dear?" "Sir, the winds trouble me." "Then rise and eat this medicine." "You too should eat, sir." "There is no discomfort for us; you eat." "Sir, while undertaking the uposatha observance I was unable to complete the whole of it; let not even my half-observance become defective." He refused to eat. "Do not act this way, dear," he was told, but even so, unwilling, as dawn was breaking, like a withered garland he passed away at that moment and was reborn in that banyan tree. Having related this matter: that setthi — a devotee of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, of the Sangha — said: "In reliance on him, as the fruit of that half-uposatha deed performed, this prosperity was obtained by me." As soon as they heard the word "Buddha," five hundred ascetics rose up, and raising their joined hands in homage to the deity, said, "Say 'Buddha'!" "I say 'Buddha'," [the deity replied], and having made them affirm this three times, [said]: "Indeed, even this sound is hard to obtain in the world," and uttered this solemn utterance: "O deities, in many hundreds of thousands of aeons, a sound never heard before has now been heard from me by you," they said. Then the pupils said this to their teacher: "Then let us go into the presence of the Teacher." The teacher [replied]: "These setthis have been of great help to us; tomorrow, having received almsfood at their dwelling and having informed them, we shall go," thus he agreed. "Very well," they assented. On the next day, the setthi, having prepared rice-gruel and food and arranged seats, knowing "today is the day our noble ones are to arrive," went out to meet them, brought them to the dwelling, seated them, and gave them alms. When they had finished their meal, they said: "Great setthi, we shall now go." [He said]: "Is it not so, venerable sirs, that you have received from us the four months' rainy-season provisions and..."

168

...gives eight kahapanas for flower-money, Khujjuttara, a slave-girl of that name, having gone to the presence of Sumanamālākāra (the garland-maker), obtains the arranged flowers. Then, on that day, the garland-maker said to her: "I have been invited by the Teacher; today I shall honor the Teacher with flowers." (Then he said:) "Just wait here for a while and be my helper in serving, having heard the Dhamma; after that you may take the remaining flowers and go." She agreed, saying "Good, good." Sumana, having served the community of monks headed by the Buddha, took the bowl for the purpose of giving thanks. The Teacher began the dhamma-discourse of thanksgiving. Khujjuttarā, merely by listening to the Teacher's dhamma-talk, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. On other days she would take four kahapanas for herself and bring back flowers worth four; but that day she brought flowers worth eight. Then Sāmāvatī said to her: "Why, mother, has the king given double the flower-money today?" "No, lady," she said. "Then why so many flowers?" "On other days, taking four kahapanas, I bought flowers with four; today why did I not keep (any for myself)?" "Having heard the Dhamma-talk of the Fully Enlightened One, and having attained the Dhamma (I did not take any for myself)." Then she (Sāmāvatī) said: "You wicked slave-girl! All this time you have been taking kahapanas (for yourself); now give them to me!" Then, scolding her, (Khujjuttarā) said: "Mother, you who have drunk the deathless yourself should also let us drink it." Having said this, she was asked, "Then bathe me," whereupon, having bathed her with sixteen pots of scented water, she had two upper cloths given to her; having put on one garment and wrapped the other over one shoulder, having prepared a seat, had a fan brought, and sitting on the seat, taking a painted fan, having summoned the five hundred women, she taught the Dhamma exactly in the manner it had been taught by the Teacher. Having heard her dhamma-talk, all of them too were established in the fruit of stream-entry. All of them, worshipping Khujjuttarā, said: "Mother, from today do not do menial work; remain in the position of our mother and teacher; go to the presence of the Teacher, and having heard whatever Dhamma is taught, tell it to us." They did accordingly. Later, she became a bearer of the Tipitaka. Then the Teacher declared: "Monks, this is the foremost among my female lay disciples who are learned, who are expounders of the Dhamma, namely Khujjuttarā."

...placed him in that foremost rank. Then those five hundred women said this: "Mother, we want to see the Teacher - show him to us," (saying) "we will honor him with garlands and perfumes and so forth"; "my dear, the royal household is such that you cannot be taken outside"; "mother, do not refuse us - just show us our Teacher"; "well then, in the walls of your private chambers, make a hole big enough to see through, and having had garlands and perfumes brought, when the Teacher is going to the house-doors of the three treasurers, stand in those various spots and look, and stretching out your hands, worship and honor him." Having done so, looking at the Teacher as he went and came, they worshipped and honored him.

Then one day Mágandiyá, coming down from her own palace terrace and walking about, went to their dwelling place and saw the hole in the room. Asking "what is this?", they - not knowing of her murderous grudge against the Teacher - said: "The Teacher has come to this city; we stand here and both see and honor him." When this was said, she thought: "So the ascetic Gotama has indeed come to this city. Now I shall know what must be done about him; and these women too are his supporters - I shall know what must be done about them as well." Thinking thus, she reported to the king: "Great king, there is a plot by the followers of Sámavatí from outside the palace; within a few days they will take your life." The king, thinking "they would not do such a thing," did not believe her. Even when told a second time he still did not believe it. Then, when told a third time and still not believing, she said: "If you do not believe me, great king, go yourself to their dwelling place and find out." The king went, saw the hole in the rooms, and asked "what is this?" When the matter was explained to him, without anger and without wrath toward them, and without saying anything, he had the holes blocked up - and it is said that at that time skylight-vents arose in all the rooms instead. Mágandiyá, unable to do anything against them, thought: "I shall do what must be done to the ascetic Gotama," and gave a bribe to the citizens, saying: "When the ascetic Gotama enters the city and walks about, abuse him and revile him together with the slaves, workmen, and servants, and drive him off." Those of false views, who had no faith in the Three Jewels, entered the city...

Having followed the Teacher [with abuse, saying]: "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are stupid, you are a camel, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are bound for hell, you are an animal — there is no good destiny for you, only a bad destiny is to be expected for you" — with these ten kinds of abusive terms they reviled and insulted him. Hearing this, the venerable Ananda said this to the Teacher: "Venerable sir, these towns-people are reviling and insulting us; let us go elsewhere from here." "Where, Ananda?" "To another town, venerable sir." "If the people there also revile us, where shall we go then, Ananda?" "To yet another town, venerable sir." "If the people there also revile us, where shall we go?" "To yet another town again, venerable sir." "It is not proper to act in this way, Ananda. Wherever a dispute has arisen, it should be settled right there where it arose; only after it is settled is it proper to go elsewhere. But who, Ananda, are these who revile [us]?" "Venerable sir, taking in slaves and servants, they all revile [us]." "I, Ananda, [bear it] as [an elephant that has] descended into battle [bears] arrows that come from the four directions — such is likewise my burden to bear the ill-spoken words of the many wicked." So saying, and taking himself as the example, teaching the Dhamma, he uttered these three verses found in the Nāgavagga:

As an elephant in battle endures the arrow shot from the bow when it falls [upon him], so shall I endure abusive speech, for many people are of bad conduct.

They lead the tamed one to an assembly, the tamed one a king mounts; best among men is the tamed one who endures abusive speech.

Excellent are tamed mules, and excellent thoroughbred Sindh horses, and excellent great tusked elephants, but better than these is the one who has tamed himself.

The teaching of the Dhamma was beneficial to the people who had assembled. Having taught the Dhamma thus, [the Buddha said]: "Do not worry, Ananda; these people will revile [us] for only seven days; on the eighth day they will be silent, for a dispute that arises concerning the Buddhas does not go on beyond seven days." Magandiya, unable to get the Teacher reviled and driven away, thought: "What indeed shall I do now?" and thinking "These [men] are the ones who support him; I shall bring ruin upon them," one day, while attending upon the king at the place where he was drinking liquor, sent a message to her uncle: "It seems there are eight things concerning the dead..." [continues]

"Let him take eight living fowls and come; and having come, let him stand at the top of the stairs, announce his arrival, and then enter" - though told this, without entering he was to first send eight living fowls ahead, and the rest afterward. To the young attendant he gave a bribe, saying, "Do as I say."

Magandiko, having come, was told, "Announce yourself to the king and enter," but he said, "I will not enter the king's drinking-hall." He sent the other young attendant, saying, "Go, dear, to my uncle's presence." That one went, and bringing the eight living fowls given by him, said, "Your majesty, a gift has been sent by the chaplain." The king said, "Indeed a fine extra dish has come to us; now who could cook it?"

Magandiya said, "Great king, the five hundred women headed by Samavati wander about with nothing to do; send it to them - they will cook it and bring it." The king said, "Go, give it to them, saying that they themselves, without putting it into anyone else's hands, must kill and cook it themselves" - and so sent it.

The young attendant said, "Very well, your majesty," went and spoke accordingly, but being refused by them with the words, "We do not commit the killing of living beings," he returned and reported the matter to the king.

Magandika said, "Great king, now by this very test you will know whether or not they commit the killing of living beings. Tell them, your majesty, to cook it and send it to the ascetic Gotama." The king spoke accordingly and sent the message.

The other messenger, pretending to go off with the fowls, instead gave those fowls to the chaplain, and brought dead fowls to the women's presence, saying, "They say, cook these fowls and send them to the Teacher's presence." The women said, "This indeed is our proper duty," and came forward and took them.

He went back to the king, and when asked, "What happened, dear?" he reported, "As soon as I said 'cook them and send to the ascetic Gotama,' they came out along the path to meet me and took the fowls."

Magandiya said, "See, great king, they do not act so for one like you; their longing lies elsewhere." When this was said, would he not believe it? The king, having heard it, endured it and remained silent.

Magandiya thought, "Now what shall I do?" At that time the king used to spend seven days in turn at the palace terrace of each of the three women - Samavati, Vasuladatta, and Magandiya. Then, knowing that tomorrow or the day after he would go to Samavati's palace terrace, Magandiya sent a message to her uncle: "Having washed the fangs [of a snake] with poison/medicine, [attach] one..."

"Let the snake be sent" -- so he said, and having done so, he sent it. The king, taking with him only his own travelling implements for his elephant-journey, set out. Now in its (the vina's) hollow there was a single hole. Magandiyá had the snake put in through that hole, and then stopped up the hole with a bunch of flowers. The snake remained shut up inside for two or three days.

On the day of the king's departure, Magandiyá asked, "To whose palace will you go today, my lord?" On being told, "To Sámavatí's," she said, "Today I saw an unlucky dream; it is not possible to go there, my lord." He replied, "I shall go all the same." She tried to restrain him up to three times, but when he would not be turned back, she said, "Since it is so, I too shall go with you," and although attempts were made to turn her back, she would not turn back, saying, "I do not know what will happen, my lord," and so she went along with the king.

The king, having put on the garments, flowers, perfumes, and ornaments given by Sámavatí and her attendants, ate a fine meal, placed the lute at the head of the couch, and lay down to sleep. Magandiyá, pretending to be walking back and forth, removed the plug of flowers from the hole of the lute. The snake, which had been without food for two or three days, came out through that hole, and seeing (them there), spread its hood and lay upon the surface of the couch.

Magandiyá, seeing it, cried out loudly, "My lord, a snake!" and, abusing both the king and (Sámavatí), said: "This foolish, unlucky king will not listen to my words! These ill-starred, wicked women -- what is it that cannot be had in the king's presence? You would live happily only if he were dead; while he lives, you live in misery. Today I saw an evil dream warning that going to Sámavatí's palace would not turn out well -- yet though I cried out, my voice was not heeded by you, my lord."

The king, seeing the snake, was terrified with fear of death, and thought: "Indeed, this is just the sort of thing these women would do! Oh, the wicked creatures! Even when she told me of their wickedness, I did not believe her words. First they made holes in their own chambers and sat there; then, when I sent fowls, they let them go; and now today they have let loose a snake on my couch!" -- and he blazed up with anger.

Sámavatí then gave this counsel to the five hundred women: "Dear ones, we have no other refuge. Towards the king, towards the queen, and towards ourselves, cultivate equal loving-kindness; be angry with no one."

The king, taking up his bow of a thousand men's strength, twanged the bowstring, and fitted a poison-smeared (arrow)...

173

Having strung the arrow, having placed Sāmāvatī at a distance, having arranged all [the women] in order and stationed them, he shot the arrow at Sāmāvatī's breast. That arrow, through the power of her loving-kindness, turned back, came facing the path by which it had come, and stopped as though it were entering her heart. The king thought: "This arrow, shot by me, pierces through even a wall; there is nothing in the sky that can stop it. Yet now it has turned back and come facing me! Surely this arrow, though fixed and lifeless, knows her virtue—while I, though a human being, do not know it!" So saying, he threw down his bow, raised his joined palms in homage, and crouching at Sāmāvatī's feet, sat on his haunches and spoke this verse:

"I am utterly confounded, bewildered; all my counsellors are bewildered.
Sāmāvatī, save me, and be my refuge."

Having heard his words, she, instead of saying "It is well, O king, go for refuge to me," said: "Great king, go for the very refuge to which I myself have gone." Having said this, Sāmāvatī [said further]: "Go for refuge to the Fully Enlightened One, free of passion—

go, O king, for that refuge to which I have gone;
this is the Buddha, great king, this is the Buddha unsurpassed.
Go for refuge to the Buddha, and you be my refuge."

So she spoke. The king, now even more afraid than before, said, uttering this verse:

"I am even more confounded; all my counsellors are bewildered.
Sāmāvatī, save me, and be my refuge."

Then she, refusing him again in the same manner as before, said: "For that reason, go for refuge to the Teacher, and I will grant you a boon." When this was said, [the king] replied: "Let the boon be accepted, great king" — he then approached the Teacher, took refuge, invited him, and gave for seven days a gift to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Addressing Sāmāvatī, he said: "Arise and take your boon." [She replied:] "Yes, great king, I have no need of gold or the like; but grant me this boon: arrange that the Teacher regularly comes here with five hundred monks, so that I may hear the Dhamma." The king, having paid homage to the Teacher, said: "Venerable sir, please come here regularly with five hundred monks," together with Sāmāvatī...

Thinking thus — "What indeed shall I do?" — she thought, "Here is a means," and sent word to the young tutor through the instruction given while going to the pleasure-garden: "Having gone to Samavati's palace, have the cloth-storeroom and the oil-storeroom opened; having soaked the cloths in the oil-vats, wrap the pillars with them; having gathered them all together, close the door, hand it over to the outer keeper, and setting fire to the house with torches, go down and depart."

He climbed up to the palace, opened the storerooms, soaked the cloths in the oil-vats, and began to wrap the pillars. Then the women headed by Samavati, saying, "What is this, young tutor?" approached him. [He said:] "Mother, the king, in order to strengthen [the pillars], has them wrapped with oil-soaked rags; in Rajagaha indeed, things ill-arranged bring about bad results — do not stay near me, mothers." Having said this, when they had come, he had them enter their chambers, closed the doors, handed [the key] to the outer keeper, and beginning from the front, setting the fire, went down.

Samavati gave them this instruction: "As we have wandered in this beginningless round of existence, so again and again have we been burned by fire in this very body; it is not an easy thing to cut off even by the Buddha's own knowledge — be heedful." While the house was burning, as they applied their minds to the meditation-subject of comprehending feelings, some attained the second fruit, some the third fruit; therefore it is said [as follows].

Then several monks, having gone for alms, returned after the meal and went to where the Blessed One was; having approached, they saluted the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: "Here, venerable sir, while King Udena had gone to the pleasure-garden, the inner palace was burned down; five hundred women headed by Samavati have died. What, venerable sir, is the destiny, what is the future state of those female lay-disciples?"

"There are here, monks, female lay-disciples who are stream-enterers; there are once-returners; there are non-returners. All those female lay-disciples, monks, did not die without fruit."

Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:

"The world, bound by delusion, appears as though it were something worthwhile;
the fool, bound by attachment, is surrounded by darkness —
it seems as if everlasting, but to one who truly sees, there is nothing [to hold onto]."

176

And having said this, he taught the Dhamma thus: "Monks, beings who go about growing up, being constantly heedless, do not perform meritorious deeds at all; being negligent, they also do evil deeds; therefore, going about growing up, they experience both pleasure and pain."

The king, it is said, having heard that Sāmāvatī's house was on fire, hurried there as fast as he could, but could not reach it in time. Having come to the house after it had already burned out, overwhelmed by a great sorrow that had arisen, he sat down surrounded by his ministers, and recalling Sāmāvatī's virtues, he thought: "Whose deed could this be?" Having reflected, he realized: "This must surely be the work of Māgandiyā." But thinking, "If I ask her directly she will not tell me; I will question her gently, by a stratagem," he said to his ministers: "Sirs, ever since long ago I have always been apprehensive and suspicious, rising up and standing watchful; she was always seeking an opportunity against me. Now, however, my mind will be at ease, and I shall be able to sleep in comfort. But by whom, O lord, was this deed done? If it was done by anyone out of love for me..." At this, Māgandiyā, standing nearby, said: "Who else could do such a thing? It was done by me, O king; I had my uncle carry it out at my command." Having said this, the king declared: "Apart from you, no one else is so devoted to me; I am pleased, and I grant you a boon; summon your own relatives." She sent word to her kinsfolk: "The king is pleased with me and grants me a boon; come quickly." When they arrived, the king showed them great honor. Seeing this, even people unrelated to her, having paid bribes, came forward claiming, "We are Māgandiyā's relatives." The king had them all seized and, in the palace courtyard, in a place not too exposed, had pits dug; he had them seated in the pits, had earth packed around them up to the waist, had straw scattered over them, and had it set on fire. When their skin had been burnt, he had them scraped with iron rakes, cutting them to pieces bit by bit. As for Māgandiyā's own body, he had flesh cut off from the fleshy parts with a sharp knife, piece by piece, placed it in an oil pan set upon an oven, had it fried like cakes, and made her eat it herself.

In the hall of Dhamma, the monks raised a discussion, saying: "Surely such a death is most unfitting for a lay devotee so endowed with faith!" The Teacher came and asked: "Monks, what discussion are you having now..."

"Having asked 'who is sitting?' and been told 'it is such-and-such,' [the Teacher said]: Monks, in this existence, this misfortune befell the women headed by Sámavatí; it was undeserved, yet it was exactly the fitting result of deeds done by them before, obtained by them here as it should have been." Having said this, when asked, "But Lord, what deed was done by them before? Please tell us," he, being requested, related a story of the past:

"Long ago, in Báráṇasí, while Brahmadatta was ruling the kingdom, eight paccekabuddhas regularly took their meals in a lodging in Rajagaha, attended by five hundred women. Of these, seven persons went to the Himalayas, and one — there was a certain clump of grass on the riverbank — having entered into meditation (jhána), sat down there. Then one day, while the king had gone off among the paccekabuddhas, those women, taking [things], went to play in the water by the riverbank. There, having played in the water for the day and come up, chilled and shivering, wanting to warm themselves, they looked around for a place to make a fire for themselves. Wandering here and there, they saw that clump of grass, and, taking it for a heap of grass, they surrounded it and stood around it, and set it on fire. As the grass burned and was falling, they saw the paccekabuddha and said: 'It is not us, it is not us! The king's paccekabuddha is burning! If the king finds out, he will have us killed! Let's make sure he is well and truly burnt!' So all of them, from here and there, brought wood and piled it up on top of him, until there was a huge pile of wood. Then, thinking 'Now, having set him alight, he will surely burn,' they went away. At first they had acted without intention, but now they had bound themselves by deliberate action. But the paccekabuddha, being in deep meditative attainment (samápatti), could not be harmed — even though they brought a thousand cartloads of wood and set it alight again and again, they could not manage to raise even the heat of his body. So, on the seventh day, he rose up and went away at his ease. Because of that deed, those women, having been cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, by the remainder (or result) of that same deed, in a hundred later existences, were burned exactly as they had burned him when their house caught fire — this was their former deed."

When this was said, the monks asked the Teacher further: "But Lord, by what deed was Khujjuttará born a hunchback? By what deed did she become very wise? By what deed did she attain the fruit of stream-entry? By what deed did she become a messenger for others?" [The Teacher replied]: "Monks, during the reign of that same king in Báráṇasí, a certain paccekabuddha, somewhat hunchbacked by nature...

...monks, having asked, "Is this what is now being discussed, having come together?" and being told, "It is so named," he said: "Monks, whatever beings are heedless, even though they live a hundred years, are indeed called dead; whatever beings are heedful, even though dead, are indeed called undying. Therefore, Magandiya and her parents, though alive, are indeed called dead, while Samavati and her retinue, though dead, are indeed called living. Monks, the heedful are not said to die." Having said this, he spoke these verses: "Heedfulness..." etc.

Herein, the word "heedfulness" illuminates a great meaning; it conveys a great meaning and stands firm in it; indeed the whole of the Buddha's teaching in the Three Baskets, when brought forth and expounded, comes down to heedfulness alone; ... "whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness... heedfulness is declared to be the foremost of those states."

Now this [heedfulness], in its essential sense, is called "the non-absence of mindfulness"; it is a name for mindfulness that is constantly established.

"The path/state of the deathless" — Nibbana is called "the deathless," for since it is unborn, it does not age and does not die; therefore it is called "deathless." "State/path" means that by this one attains the deathless state — it is said to be the means of attaining the deathless.

"Heedlessness" is the state of negligence; it is a name for the relinquishing of mindfulness, described as forgetfulness of truth. ... "Path/state" means the way, the path.

For the heedless person does not escape birth; having been born, he ages and dies; thus heedlessness is called "the path/state of death," for beings go to death [through it].

"The heedful do not die" — those endowed with mindfulness, being heedful, indeed do not die; but it should not be understood that they become ageless and deathless, for there is no being at all called ageless and deathless. Rather, for the heedless, what is called growth [of the round of rebirth] is unlimited, while for the heedful it is limited. Therefore the heedless, being unreleased from birth and so forth, are indeed called "dead" both while living and when dead. But the heedful, having developed the characteristic of heedfulness, quickly realize the paths and fruits, and are not reborn in a second or third existence; therefore they, whether living or dead, are indeed called "not dying."

"The heedless are as if dead" — whatever beings are heedless, they are dead through the death of heedlessness; for just as those who are dead through the severance of the life faculty become like logs of wood, devoid of consciousness, so too [the heedless] become exactly the same; indeed, for all of them, just as for those who are truly dead...

180

"We shall give this gift," "we shall keep this precept" — thinking thus, a single thought does not arise even once; (likewise) for those who have gone forth, "we shall fulfill the duties toward preceptors and teachers," "we shall undertake the ascetic practices" (dhutanga, etc.), "we shall develop meditation" — thinking thus, not even a single thought arises; by this measure (or: by mattena?) they become [spiritually] diminished. Hence it is said: "those who are heedless, as they are heedless" — having known this distinction specifically, it is said: there is no escape for one who is heedless; the existence [of escape] belongs to the one who is heedful — having known this distinction specifically; now, who are those who know this distinction? — "the wise among the heedful" means those who are wise, intelligent (c. -i), possessed of living wisdom (or: possessed of wisdom together with life?); standing firm in heedfulness themselves, they increase heedfulness; thus they know this special cause... Of the noble ones — Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples — dwelling, delighting, and rejoicing in the field reckoned as the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, in the thirty-seven qualities pertaining to enlightenment, in the ninefold supramundane state — this is the meaning; "those who meditate" means those heedful wise ones who meditate by either of the two kinds of meditation: the meditation of close contemplation reckoned as attainment of concentration, or the meditation of close contemplation reckoned as insight, path, and fruit; "constantly" means that from the time of going forth until the path of arahantship, bodily, mental, and volitional energy is continuously active;... "they touch" — here there are two kinds of touching: the touching through knowledge and the touching through result (vipāka); among these, the four paths are called "touching through knowledge," and the four fruits are meant as "touching through result"; the wise, the learned, realizing Nibbāna by the noble fruit, realize Nibbāna by that touching through result; "the supreme security from bondage" means: the four bonds that sink and submerge the great mass of people — security and freedom from fear from these, through all mundane and supramundane states, being supreme, is called "the unsurpassed"... This is the Udena story illustrating the conduct of Sāmāvatī and Māgandiyā.

"Appamādo amatapadam" should be read as "appamādo 'matapadam," on the model of verse 24 "yaso 'bhivaddhati," verses 134, 154 "patto 'si," "ditṭho 'si," verse 821 "yo 'tivākyam," verse 851 "antimo 'yam." Compare "amatapadam" with verse 114 "amatam padam." "Ariyānam" — of the noble, the excellent, i.e., of the virtuous, the perfected; the Pali [word]...

181

for indeed this word seems to be used especially in a moral sense in language. Cfr. vv. 79. 164. 190-91. 270. 208, and the book called the Suttanipáta, chapter Dvayatánupassanásuttam, with reference to Dhpd. v. 6,

"What others call happiness, that the noble ones call suffering,
what others call suffering, that the noble ones know as happiness."

The commentary understands this as spoken of the three orders: buddhas, paccekabuddhas, and disciples (sávaka). Cfr. Burnouf: Introd. p. 290, and also Lassen: Indische Alterthumskunde I, p. 5, and Nève: Le mythe des Ribhavas p. 117.

... "One who acts with deliberation" means: thinking "if it shall be so, I shall act thus," having in this very act considered beforehand, as it were, the cause from which "it shall be known as such-and-such" would arise, like a physician treating a disease by carefully observing and considering it (? read: treating sickness) — [thus] one who, having considered and examined all actions, performs them accordingly; ... Gogerly (cf. Knighton p. 78) translates verse 27 thus: Live
not in the practice of irreligion, neither cleave to sensuality;
for the meditative and the religious man experiences great
happiness.


v. 28. The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this teaching of the Dhamma beginning "Heedlessness, by heedfulness..." with reference to the Elder Mahākassapa. For one day, that Elder, while dwelling at the Pipphali Cave, having returned from his alms-round in Rājagaha, developed [the divine eye] and sat surveying with it the beings — whether heedless or heedful — who were passing away and arising in the waters, on the earth, on the mountains, and so forth. The Teacher, seated at Jetavana, surveying with the divine eye [and wondering], "In what dwelling is my son Kassapa staying today?", beheld him sitting and surveying the passing-away and rebirth of beings, and knowing this, thought: "The passing-away and rebirth of beings cannot be fully comprehended even by the knowledge of a Buddha; without the conception in the mother's womb being taken into account, and without the parents being made aware, no determination can be made of beings who are passing away. To know this lies beyond even your scope, Kassapa — it is not your province; but to know and to see completely the beings who everywhere are passing away and arising is the province of Buddhas alone." Having said this, he sent forth a radiance, and, as though seated face to face with him, spoke this verse: "Heedlessness, by heedfulness," and so on.

Here, as to the word "drives out" (nudati): just as someone entering a lotus pond with fresh water, having stirred up the old water and given it no further place, drives it to flee away over its own surface — so too the wise man, cultivating the mark of heedfulness, gives no place to heedlessness, and by the force of heedfulness drives it out. Then, with heedlessness thus driven away, having purified the divine eye, reckoned as supreme through wisdom, fulfilling the practice that befits it, and by means of that practice ascending as though by a staircase to a palace, being free from the dart of sorrow, sorrowless, [he contemplates] the sorrowful generation, the mass of beings, as they pass away...

...and sees, with the divine eye, both what is arising and what is passing away. As for example: one who stands at the top of a mountain, standing on the mountain-top, looking down upon beings standing on the ground below in various palaces and terraces without effort — in the same way the wise one, the learned one, the great destroyer of the taints (mahákhíṇásavo), observes fools, whose seeds of growth have not been cut off, both as they pass away and as they arise.

v. 29. Setting: Jetavana. Characters: two companion monks.

...Among the sutras: through the absence of mindful wakefulness, while all are asleep in every bodily posture; "wide awake" means: standing established in abundant wakefulness of mindfulness; "weak" means: like a worn-out, lame, feeble horse compared to a swift, thoroughbred steed; "wise" (sumedhaso) means: a person of the highest wisdom who proceeds leaving behind [others] both by approach and by attainment. For when one of little wisdom is striving to grasp a single sutta, the wise one grasps a whole section (or: path) and thus proceeds by mere approach. And for one of little wisdom, while striving to accomplish such things as establishing day and night retreats, the wise one — having already learned the meditation subject and having recited it — having also entered beforehand into the day and night retreats made ready by another, reflecting upon the meditation subject, having destroyed all defilements, brings the nine supramundane states into his grasp; thus he proceeds by attainment, leaving others behind. But when it has grown (vaddhe), having left it, having abandoned it, he proceeds, going forth from what has grown.

The construction of this verse does not appear altogether accurate; for it is scarcely permissible to draw the gerund "hitvá" into a comparative statement, and as referred to the primary statement, it lacks an object; it should have read: "the heedful one, leaving the heedless behind... proceeds."

v. 30. "By heedfulness, Maghavá..." — this teaching of the Dhamma the Teacher, while dwelling near Vesáli in the Kúṭágárasálá, gave with reference to Sakka, the king of the gods. For at Vesáli there was a Licchavi named Maháli, who, [having heard] the Tathágata's teaching of the Sakkapañha Sutta...

Having heard this, the Fully Enlightened One, having made much of Sakka's great attainment, told it. Then thinking, "Has he seen, or has he not seen? Does he know, or does he not know? I will ask him" — thus thinking, Mahali the Licchavi then approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he saluted the Blessed One and sat down on one side. Sitting on one side, Mahali said this to the Blessed One: "Has the Blessed One seen Sakka, lord of the gods? Has Mahali indeed seen Sakka, lord of the gods?" "Surely that must have been something resembling Sakka, for Sakka, lord of the gods, is hard to see, lord." "I know Sakka, Mahali, in the performing of what is Sakka's duty, and I know the qualities by undertaking which Sakka attained Sakka-hood, and... I know. Sakka, Mahali, lord of the gods, formerly, when he was a human being, was a young man named Magha; therefore he is called Maghavā. Sakka, Mahali, lord of the gods, formerly, when he was a human being, gave gifts in town after town; therefore he is called Purindada. Sakka, Mahali, lord of the gods, formerly, when he was a human being, gave gifts respectfully; therefore he is called Sakka. Sakka, Mahali, lord of the gods, formerly, when he was a human being, gave a dwelling place; therefore he is called Vāsava. Sakka, Mahali, lord of the gods, thought out the meaning of a thousand matters in a single moment; therefore he is called Sahassakkha. Sakka's, Mahali, lord of the gods', chief consort is named Sujātā, daughter of the asuras; therefore he is called Sujampati. Sakka, Mahali, lord of the gods, exercises sovereign rule as foremost over the Tāvatimsa gods; therefore he is called Devānam Indo (Lord of the Gods). Sakka's, Mahali, lord of the gods', formerly, when he was a human being, seven vows were undertaken fully and completely, and by undertaking them Sakka attained Sakka-hood. What are the seven? 'As long as I live, may I support my mother and father; as long as I live, may I honor the eldest in the family; as long as I live, may I speak gently; as long as I live, may I be free of slander; as long as I live, may I dwell at home with a mind free from the stain of avarice, with open-handed generosity, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to giving alms, delighting in the sharing of gifts.'"

"...good." "I too will be your friend." "Be so, friend; friendship is pleasing to many." From then on there were two of them. Others, seeing this, asking and hearing the same thing, also became friends; and so on, one after another, more friends joined, until thirty-three men in all had come together. All of them, carrying small tools and the like in their hands, went about making the road level, at distances of a yojana or two yojanas apart.

Seeing them, the village headman thought: "These men are yoked to useless work. All of them might instead bring fish and meat from the forest, or make and drink liquor, or do other such things — and I too might get something out of it." So he had them summoned and asked: "What are you doing, going about like this?" "We are making the road to heaven, sir." [He said:] "Even while living the household life one can prosper by doing that — bringing fish and meat from the forest, making and drinking liquor, and carrying on various kinds of business; that too is a way to prosper." But they rejected his words. Though told again and again, they still rejected them.

He, growing angry, thought "I will destroy them," and went to the king, saying: "Your Majesty, I see thieves going about bound together in a gang." Being told, "Go, seize them and bring them here," he did so and brought them before the king. The king, without investigating, ordered: "Have them trampled by an elephant."

Magha then gave instruction to the rest: "Steady yourselves well — apart from loving-kindness we have no other refuge. Without harboring anger toward anyone, be of loving mind and even mind toward the king, the village headman, the trampling elephant, and yourselves." They did so.

Then, through the power of their loving-kindness, the elephant could not bear to approach them. The king, hearing of this, and seeing the large crowd, thought "he will not be able to trample them," and said: "Go, cover them with mats and have them trampled." When they were brought covered with mats to be trampled, the elephant, though driven on, backed away from a distance.

The king, hearing this report, thought "there must be some reason for this," and had them summoned and asked: "Relying on what do you... (?)..." "What is this, Your Majesty?" "It is said that you go about in the forest as thieves bound together in a gang." "Who said this?" "The village headman, sire." "We are not thieves, Your Majesty; we, clearing our own path to heaven, do this and that" — [thus the] village...

The feeder, having set us to an unwholesome deed and trying to impose his own will, wanting to drive [the elephant] away, grew angry and spoke thus; "Father (c.-a), this elephant knows your worth, but being reborn as a human I could not recognize it—forgive me." Having said this, he then gave to them the village together with its sons and wives and food, the elephant fit to be mounted, and the village for their free enjoyment, saying, "Here indeed the reward of our meritorious deed is seen." Being filled with ever greater (c. ever more fearful) faith of mind, and mounting that elephant turn by turn as they went along, they discussed among themselves: "Now we should do an even greater act of merit—what shall we do?" They decided, "At the crossroads we will build a permanent resting-hall (c. shelter) for the people," and summoning a carpenter, they had a hall built. But as for women, being free of desire (?) [for them], they gave the women no share in that hall.

Now in Magha's house there were four women—Nandá, Cittá, Sudhammá, and Sujátá. Among them, Sudhammá, joining with the carpenter, said, "Brother, make me chief one in this hall," and gave him a bribe. He agreed, saying "Good," and first had the central pillar-tree dried, trimmed, and bored, and having finished the capital [of the pillar], carved on it the words "This hall is named Sudhammá," then wrapped it in cloth and set it aside. Then, when the hall was finished, on the day appointed for raising the capital, [someone said], "Sirs, sirs, we have forgotten one thing (?)" — "What is it?" — "The capital." — "We will fetch it." — "Now it cannot be made from a newly cut tree; but since one was cut and set aside earlier, it can be obtained." — "Now what should be done?" — "If in anyone's house there is a finished, ready-made capital for sale (?), it should be sought." They went searching and, seeing one in Sudhammá's house, offered a thousand [coins] but could not get it for that price. [She said]: "If you give me a share in the hall, I will give it to you." When this was said, they replied, "We will not give a share to a woman." Then the carpenter said to them: "Sirs, what are you doing? Apart from the Brahma-world, there is no place called 'free of women'—take the capital. If you do so, our work will come to completion." They agreed, saying "Good," took the capital, finished the hall, and divided it into three parts, in one portion being the dwelling of the lords...

...they made [shelters], one for the destitute, one for the sick.

The thirty-three men had thirty-three plank-seats made, and gave a sign to the elephant (c. -thi, "sign"): "When a visitor arrives and sits down on whichever plank-seat, take him and install him in the house of the owner of that plank-seat; all the care of his feet, care of his back, food both hard and soft, and lodging shall be the responsibility of that owner alone." The elephant (c. -i) would take whoever came and went and lead him to the house of the owner of the plank, and that owner would carry out his duty for that day.

Magha planted a kovilára tree not far from the hall and spread a stone slab at its foot. When the hall was finished, finished, [someone] looked at the finial, read the letters, [and found]: "They say this hall, named Sudhammá, is mine (?)" — but the names of the thirty-three men were not made known.

Nandá (or Náná) thought: "These people building the hall left me out without any share; but Sudhammá, through her own cleverness, has gained a share. What can I also do to gain merit? What indeed shall I do?" Then this thought occurred to her: "It would increase [merit] if those who come to the hall could obtain water to drink and water for washing" — [thinking] "I shall have a pool dug," she had a pool made.

Cittá thought: "A finial was given by Sudhammá, a pool was made by Nandá; what can I also do to gain merit? What indeed shall I do?" Then this thought occurred to her: "Those who come to the hall, after drinking water and bathing, when they go on their way, like to wear garlands — it would increase [merit] — I shall have a flower garden made." She had a lovely flower garden made, so that for the most part in that garden there was no tree without flowers and fruit.

But Sujátá said: "I alone am Magha's maternal uncle's daughter, and I alone wait upon his feet; therefore whatever has been done belongs to me, it was done by me" — thinking thus, she did nothing at all, and spent her time merely adorning her own person.

Magha himself, having fulfilled these seven vows — support of mother and father, honoring the elders of the family, truthful speech, speech free from harshness, speech free from slander, freedom from stinginess, and freedom from anger —

[recited the verse:]
"One who supports mother and father, who honors the elders of the family,
whose speech is gentle and kindly, who has given up slander,"

...is an elephant, he fashions for the thirty-three (gods) thirty-three vessels (domed pavilions). In a courtyard measuring half a league to a league, in the midst of all of them, for Sakka's sake he fashions the vessel called Sudassana, thirty yojanas (wide). Above it stands a jewelled pavilion twelve yojanas (high); there, here and there, banners made of the seven kinds of jewels, a yojana high, rise up; at its edges hangs a network of little bells; it has a pleasant breeze-pavilion (?); and from it issues forth the sound of divine music mingled with the sound of the five kinds of instruments. In the middle of the pavilion a jewelled couch of the proper sort is prepared for Sakka; there Sakka sits. In each one of the thirty-three vessels he fashions seven tusks, each fifty yojanas long. In each (tusk?) there are forty-nine lotus-ponds; in each lotus-pond there are seven clusters of lotus-plants; in each cluster there are seven flowers; on each flower there are forty-nine petals; on each petal seven divine maidens dance. Thus, all around, within that fifty-yojana area, right up to the elephant's tusks, there is the sound of dancing. Enjoying such great glory, Sakka, king of the gods, moves about.

Sudhammā too, having died, went and was reborn there; then there arose a divine assembly-hall named Sudhammā, nine hundred yojanas (in extent). They say there is no place more delightful than this. On the eighth day of the month, the hearing of the Dhamma takes place there. Even today, when people see a delightful place, they say it is like the Sudhammā assembly-hall.

Nandā too, having died, was reborn there; for her there arose a lotus-pond named Nandā, five hundred yojanas (in extent).

Cittā, having died, went and was reborn there; for her too there arose a grove called Cittalatā, five hundred yojanas (in extent); there, the young gods who were born there, overcome by its wonders, wander about enchanted.

Sujātā, however, having died, was reborn as a heron in a certain mountain ravine.

Sakka, looking over his attendants, thought: "Sudhammā has indeed been reborn here, likewise Nandā and Cittā — but where, I wonder, has Sujātā been reborn?" Thinking thus, he saw that she had been reborn there (as a heron), and thought: "The foolish woman, having done no merit, has been reborn in an animal womb. Now, however, having had her perform merit, I will bring her here and let her prosper." So thinking, he changed/assumed [another] form...

...having left [her appearance] disguised as an unknown person, having gone to her presence, [he] asked "What are you doing here, wandering about?"; "But who are you?"; "I am your husband, Magha"; "Where were you reborn?"; "I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; do you know the place where your companions were reborn?"; "I do not know, sir"; "They too were reborn right near me; you will see your companions"; "How shall I go there?"; Sakka, saying "I will take you there," placed her on his palm, took her to the heaven-world, and having released her at Nanda's lotus pond, announced to the other three: "You will see your companion Sujātā"; "Where is that goddess?"; "At the edge of Nandā's lotus pond," [he said]; those three having gone there [said]: "Oh, this is the fruit of adorning one's own body in such a way! Look at the ... (?), look at the feet, look at the calves, how beautiful is this form!" — having made this joking remark, they departed. Again Sakka, having gone to her presence, said "Your companions have seen you," [and she] having seen [them said], "Having lifted me up, take me right there"; when this was said, he took her right there and released her into the water; having seen [her], he asked "Have your companions seen your attainment?"; "The goddesses have seen it"; "You too should strive to achieve rebirth there"; "What should I do, lord?"; "Will you keep the precept I give you?"; "I will keep it, lord"; then having given her the five precepts, he said, "Guard them carefully," and departed; from then on she herself sought out and ate only dead fish. Sakka, after a few days, in order to test her, went and lay down on the sand looking like a dead fish; she, seeing it, took it thinking "a dead fish"; the fish, at the time of being swallowed, moved its tail; she, thinking "it's alive," released it into the water; he, after a while, again lay belly-up in front of her; again she, thinking "it's dead," took it, but seeing it move its gills at the time of swallowing, she released it thinking "it's a live fish"; having thus tested her three times [and found that] she kept the precept well, he made himself known [saying]: "I came to test you; you keep the precept well; keeping it thus, before long you will be reborn in my presence; be heedful," and departed. From then on, she herself would get a dead fish or not; not getting one, after just a few days...

...not having obtained [a match], [they said]: "This one is now unsuitable for the granddaughter of her grandfather, being old" — and, embarrassed, they went away. Sakka seized him/her by the hand, shouted "I am indeed [Sakka]!" and leapt up into the sky. The asuras, [realizing] "we have been deceived by old Sakka," pursued him. Mátali the charioteer, having brought the Vejayanta chariot, stood waiting in the middle of the road. Sakka mounted it there and sped off toward the city of the gods. Then, when it reached the silk-cotton forest, the young garudas, frightened on hearing the sound of the chariot, cried out. Hearing their cries, Sakka asked Mátali: "Who are these crying out?" "They are garuda deities." "For what reason?" "They cried out from fear of death on hearing the sound of the chariot." [Sakka said:] "Because of me alone, so many creatures are being crushed by the speed of the chariot — do not let them perish; turn the chariot back." He gave the signal with the goad to the thousand Sindh horses and turned the chariot around.

Seeing this, the asuras said: "Old Sakka, who was fleeing from the city of the asuras, has now turned his chariot back — surely he must have gained support from elsewhere and will [return to fight]." Thinking so, they turned back and entered the asura city by the way they had come, and again raised their heads [in pride].

He took Suja, the asura maiden, to the city of the gods and installed her as chief among the two-and-a-half-crore nymphs. She asked a boon of Sakka: "Great king, I have no mother or father, no brothers or sisters in this heavenly world — wherever you go, take me along with you." He said, "Very well," and gave her his promise.

From then on, whenever the coral tree blossomed, [the asuras would say]: "Now is the season for our heavenly Páricchattaka tree to bloom" — and the asuras would march out to make war on Sakka. Sakka assigned protection of the ocean below to the nagas; then to the garudas, the kumbhandas, and the yakkhas; and to the Four Great Kings he gave good attendants (?). At the gates of the city of the gods he stationed vajra-handed guardians, and set up an image of Indra. Even when the asuras, having cut down the nagas and the rest, came on, upon seeing the image of Indra they would cry, "Sakka has come out!" and flee.

Thus the young man Mágha/Máháli followed the path of heedfulness, and being heedful, attained such lordship that he now rules over the two worlds of the gods. This heedfulness (appamáda) is indeed praised by the Buddhas and others, for it is through heedfulness that all beings attain distinction, whether worldly or supramundane. Having said this, [the Teacher] spoke this verse: "Through heedfulness..."
